en: *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Second Chapter (1.1):
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does a monk, gradually abandoning the outflows (*āsrava*), first abandon unwholesome phenomena?
He cultivates, clearly perceives, thoroughly investigates, contemplates with the mind, and establishes wholesome dharmas.
With knowledge derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

that monk [sees] how, from the very beginning, by means of those sense objects and faculties which have become mutual causes and conditions, the entire world has wandered in saṃsāra since beginningless time.
He contemplates this ocean of sense objects, which is the very cause of birth:
"By means of external and internal sense objects, this world is made to wander.
(1.3) From the very beginning, he first practices a delight in solitude.
In secluded forest thickets, groves, heaps of straw, at the roots of trees, and in cremation grounds, he practices for the purpose of binding the monkey of the mind.
The mind of one who delights in seclusion becomes serene;
he finds no delight in villages amidst laughter, frolicking, and play.
He does not become intent on looking at women, nor does he delight in socializing.
There are two courtesans for celibacy: [the one who leads away and the one who brings back].
There are two kinds of company: that of a courtesan and that of a social gathering.
He first abandons these two types of company; his mind then becomes more one-pointed and serene.
(1.4.1) He reflects thus: "How can the mind be concentrated and held steady from the very beginning?
From the very beginning, he perceives:
“The mind wanders through eighteen mental deviations, whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
(1.4.2) By which eighteen? Namely: having seen forms with the eye, ...
It becomes a basis for mental gladness;
it is defiled and has an unwholesome maturation; one experiences it and reflects upon it.
It becomes a basis for mental distress, yet he becomes dispassionate toward it;
that is his wholesome ripening.
It becomes a basis for equanimity;
it is an indeterminate maturation.
(2) (1.4.3) Likewise, having heard a sound with the ear, it becomes a basis for equanimity; it is an indeterminate maturation.
It is a basis for mental gladness,
defiled, and has an unwholesome ripening;
it is a basis for mental distress.
That which has purification as its object is wholesome and results in a pleasant ripening;
it is a basis for equanimity and results in an indeterminate ripening.
(1.4.4) Likewise, having smelled odors with the nose,
that which is a basis for mental pleasure may be defiled and result in unwholesome maturation.
It becomes a basis for mental distress;
it becomes purifying and the ripening of the wholesome;
it becomes a basis for equanimity.
It is indeterminate and results in maturation.
(1.4.5) Likewise, having tasted flavors with the tongue,
it becomes a basis for mental pleasure.

That which is associated with affliction is unwholesome and results in maturation; it is a basis for mental distress. That which is associated with purification is wholesome and results in maturation.
It becomes a basis for equanimity;
it is an indeterminate maturation.
(1.4.6) Thus, having touched a tangible object with the body...
It becomes a basis for mental pleasure,
yet it is defiled and results in unwholesome maturation;
it becomes a basis for mental pain.
It is purifying, it is the result of wholesome karma;
it is a basis for equanimity,
and it is of indeterminate fruition.
(3) (1.4.7) Having thus known phenomena with the mind, that which is a basis for mental gladness becomes something defiled and the maturation of unwholesome karma.
It becomes a basis for mental distress;
it becomes purifying, a wholesome result of maturation;
it becomes a basis for equanimity.
It is an indeterminate maturation.
(4) (1.4.8) Thus, through these eighteen mental deviations, which have three types of maturation, there occurs death and rebirth in *saṃsāra*.
(1.5.1) When that monk perceives the eighteen mental deviations,
Then the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere, being even more delighted, announce it to the yakṣas dwelling on earth;
and the yakṣas dwelling on earth and those roaming the atmosphere, with joyful minds, announce it to the four Great Kings.
Those four Great Kings then announce it to the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings:

“That son of good family from Jambūdvīpa— who, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, has out of faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life from such-and-such a village, such-and-such a town, such-and-such a district, and such-and-such a family— he, delighting in solitude and wandering alone, reflects upon and realizes the eighteen mental deviations.”
Having heard that from the presence of the four Great Kings,
the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings become even more joyful, thinking:
"The faction of Māra is declining!"
The side of the true Dharma is being uplifted.
(1.5.3) Those gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings informed Śakra, the lord of the Thirty-three, saying: "O Lord, that one who..."

From Jambudvīpa, a son of good family... [as before]... from such-and-such a family, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, has out of faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life;
he delights in solitude... [as before]... being a cemetery-dweller, he reflects upon the eighteen mental deviations.
Having realized it for himself and attained it, he dwells therein.
And having heard that from the presence of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the god Kauśika, lord of the Thirty-three, becomes even more joyful in mind.
(2.1) Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
having clearly perceived the eighteen mental deviations, what other stage does that monk realize?
He perceives this through knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye:
(2.2) He perceives four foundations:
namely, the foundation of wisdom, the foundation of truth, the foundation of relinquishment, and the foundation of tranquility.
(2.3) How does a monk practice the foundation of wisdom?
In this case, a monk perceives the body itself according to its actual state through the nature of the true Dharma;
he understands it,
analyzes it, and examines it.
“In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
(2.4.1) Among these, what is the earth element?
The earth element is twofold.
There is that which is internal and there is that which is external.

(2.4.2) Among these, what is the internal? Whatever in this body is internal, belonging to oneself, approached, and appropriated—therein, "approached" refers to the collection of skin, flesh, and so forth; "appropriated" refers to the collection of head-hair, teeth, nails, body-hair, and bones.
What, then, is that which is hard, solid, and appropriated? Namely:

(6) hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, dust, skin, flesh, bones, veins, tendons, heart, spleen, lungs, kidneys, liver, saliva, the stomach and the intestines, the small intestines, the abdominal cavity, the large intestine, and the brain.
“Or whatever else in this body is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, of a solid nature, approached, and clung to— this is called the internal earth element.
(2.4.3) In that regard, what is the external earth element?”
Whatever external hardness there is, that which is solid, not clung to, and not appropriated;
this is called the external earth element.
(2.4.4) Therein, as for the internal earth element:
And that which is external—
having condensed both together into one—
"This is a realm; it is merely a realm."
He does not view the earth element as presided over by an experiencer, nor as accidental; he views it as neither permanent nor pleasant.
“I see nothing as pure, nor as having a self.
That monk has resolute conviction based on wisdom.
“‘All this is not mine; I am not this; this is not my self.’”
“Having seen this thus as it really is with right wisdom, the mind becomes dispassionate toward the earth element.
In this way, a monk becomes one who is intent upon the foundation of wisdom.”
(2.5.1) In that regard, what is the water element (*abdhātu*)? The water element is also twofold:
there is the internal element and there is the external element.

(2.5.2) Therein, the internal [element] is whatever in this body is water, of the nature of water, belonging to the water-element, having the characteristic of moisture within the body: "sweat, (7) saliva, nasal mucus, brain, blood, fat, synovial fluid, marrow, bile, urine, and the brain-matter";
or whatever else exists in this body that is internal, personal, of the nature of water, approached, and appropriated.
This is called the internal water element. (2.5.3) What is the external [water element]?
Whatever is external, belonging to water, watery, viscous, or belonging to viscosity, which is not clung to and not appropriated.
This is called the external water element.
(2.5.4) Therein, that which is the internal water element and that which is the external—
Having condensed all that into a single whole: "This is a realm, merely a realm; none of this is mine."
"Having seen with right wisdom: 'I am not this; this is not my self,'"
The mind becomes dispassionate toward the water element.
In this way, that monk ascends to the foundation of wisdom.
(2.6.1) In that regard, what is the fire element?
The fire element is also twofold:
there is the internal and there is the external.
(2.6.2) Therein, the internal fire element is whatever in this body is internal, belonging to the self, which is fire, of the nature of fire, approached, and appropriated.
What, then, is that?
It is as follows: that by which one is tormented and that by which one is consumed with fever.
That by which one is fevered,
and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper and comfortable digestion;
Furthermore, whatever else there is in this body that is internal, belonging to oneself, which is fire, of the nature of fire, approached, and grasped— this is called the internal fire element.
(2.6.3) In that regard, what is the external fire element?
Whatever external fire, or what has become fire, is hot, of the nature of heat, approached, or grasped—
this is called the external fire element.
Therein, that which is the internal fire element, [is as follows:]
And that which is external—
having condensed both together into one—
"This is a realm; it is merely a realm."
"All this is not mine; I am not this;
this is not my self."
“Having seen this thus as it really is with right wisdom, the mind becomes dispassionate toward the fire element:
‘This is not presided over by an agent.’”
The fire element does not proceed as presided over by an experiencer.
(2.7.1) In that regard, what is the wind element?
The wind element is also twofold.
There is that which is internal and that which is external.

(2.7.2) Among these, what is the internal? Whatever in this body is internal, belonging to oneself, wind or of the nature of wind, light and mobile, and has been appropriated [as part of the organism].
Furthermore, what is that?

It is the upward-moving wind, the downward-moving wind, the lateral-moving wind, the abdominal wind; likewise, the piercing winds, the pricking winds, the cutting winds, the *vātāṣṭhīla* wind, and the eighty winds together with the openings for parasites;
and the eighty winds that follow each individual limb.

Or whatever else there is in this body that is internal, belonging to oneself, airy or of the nature of air, characterized by lightness and motion, and clung to— this is called the internal wind element.
(9) (2.7.3) In that regard, what is the external wind element?
Whatever is external— wind, that which belongs to wind, light and mobile, not reached [by consciousness], and not grasped—
this is called the external wind element. (2.7.4) Therein, as for the internal wind element:
And whatever is external—
all this, when condensed together,
is "this is a realm; it is merely a realm."
"All this is not mine;
I am not this;
this is not my self."
Having seen with right wisdom, as it truly is, that this is not presided over by an agent nor presided over by an experiencer,
one becomes dispassionate toward the wind element.
In this way, the monk becomes a witness through the foundation of wisdom.
(2.8.1) In that regard, what is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*)?
The space element is also twofold.
There is an internal [space] and there is an external [space].

(2.8.2) Therein, the internal is whatever in this body is internal, individual, space, belonging to space, approached, appropriated, unmanifest, and consisting of form that cannot be pervaded— by means of which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted enters within through its opening.

Furthermore, whatever is the cavity of the throat, the cavity of the ear, the cavity of the eye, the cavity of the nose, the cavity of the tongue, and that which is within the food providing space for the tongue—
this is called the internal space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
(2.8.3) In that regard, what is the external space element?
Whatever is in space, unapproached, unappropriated, unmanifested, and not pervaded— namely,
the hollows between the branches of trees, the hollows between mountains, the hollows of caves, grottoes, and riverbeds, or whatever external hollow there may be:
this is called the external space element.
(10) (2.8.4) Therein, whatever is the element of space pertaining to internal form and whatever is external, having condensed these together into one,
“This is a realm, merely a realm.
All this is not mine; this I am not.”
"This is not my self"—
having seen this thus as it really is with right wisdom, the mind becomes dispassionate toward the element of space.
Having seen it thus,
One does not take it up: "All this is not mine;
this is not who I am."
"This is not my self;
it is not presided over by an agent,
nor presided over by a knower."
“The mind becomes detached from the element of space.
(2.9) In that regard, what is the mind-element (*manodhātu*)? The mind-element is associated with the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*).”
One experiences with mental consciousness an object that was experienced by visual consciousness.
In this way, the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind originate from the element of mental consciousness and have the mind as their root. (11)
And there are verses on this subject:
Mental states are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are swift as the mind.
With a well-purified mind, one speaks or acts;
having shaken off the stain of evil, one understands death and rebirth.
One who knows the true nature of the fruits of actions attains the imperishable state.
One who has restrained all the senses, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, who is peaceful, self-controlled, and established in his own nature— such a person is a true mendicant.
(2.10.2) (12) Mounted upon the chariot of the six sense-faculties, he who turns back the enemy of passion—
the wise, steadfast, and active one— attains the state of peace.
Dwelling in the forest, contented, sleeping on the ground, and concentrated in mind,
he shakes off evil states just as the wind disperses clouds in the sky.

One whose speech and physical actions are pure, who is devoted to virtuous conduct, who possesses the vision of reality, and who is skillful in practice— such a person shall destroy the abode of Māra.
Passion and the like do not afflict the virtuous mind that is free from craving;
the monk who abides in the way leading to liberation is filled with abundant loving-kindness and compassion.

(2.10.6) He for whom forms and other sense objects are not desired as causes of bondage attains supreme peace, having gone where one does not grieve. (2.10.7) (13) (3.1) Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:

Has that monk first ascended from the first stage—the eighteen mental deviations—to the second stage, the stage of knowing the reality of the six elements; and now, by means of knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye, does he perceive the stage of recollecting the Dharma?
(14) (3.2) That monk, the seer of reality, enters the third stage.
What is the interval between stages? It is the interval between the stages of the mind’s precedence.
He discerns that pleasure as it arises.
He discerns suffering as it arises;
he knows mental pleasure;
he knows mental pain.
One discerns equanimity.
(3.3.1) What does one discern as pleasure?
Dependent upon a contact conducive to pleasant feeling, a pleasant feeling arises.
When experiencing a pleasant feeling, he understands as it really is: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
Then, there is the element of cessation for that contact conducive to pleasant feeling.
Experiencing the feeling arisen in dependence on a contact conducive to pleasant feeling, he recognizes the subsided feeling: "My pleasant feeling has subsided."
“My pleasant feeling has subsided;
a painful feeling has arisen for me.
He recognizes that painful feeling as having arisen dependently.

(3.3.2) “A pleasant feeling has arisen for me”—thus he recognizes it, being truly present in detail, exactly as the contact conducive to a pleasant feeling was described; the same should also be stated regarding a feeling conducive to suffering.
(3.3.3) What does one cognize as mental joy (*saumanasya*)?
“Mental pleasure arises dependent on contact that is a basis for mental pleasure.
How does he recognize mental pain?
“It arises dependent on contact that is a basis for mental pain. (15)
...mental distress.
Then, as he correctly contemplates that very feeling which is a basis for joy,
and having seen the cessation of what is a basis for joy, [he perceives]...
One becomes dispassionate toward mental joy,
thinking: "That feeling of mental joy which previously arose in me has perished, been stilled, and come to an end."
“Then, detachment arises in him,
and he realizes things as they truly are.
(3.3.4–5) The same applies to mental distress.”
The same should be said regarding equanimity as well.
(3.4) As he ascends to this third stage, the terrestrial yakṣas, being exceedingly joyful, announce it to the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere. They, in turn, announce it to the four Great Kings.
They, in turn, inform the gods of the Four Great Kings;
they also inform Kauśika Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"That noble son named so-and-so, from such-and-such a region, from such-and-such a village, and from such-and-such a family in Jambūdvīpa, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes..."
Having gone forth from the home to the homeless life out of faith, he has ascended to the third stage and desires to wage war against Māra;
the faction of Māra is being diminished.
"The side of the True Dharma is being uplifted.
(3.5) Having heard this,
Kauśika Śakra, lord of the gods, with a most joyful mind, mounted Airāvaṇa.
Taking with him a host of gods headed by Maharddhika, he informs the Yāma gods:
"A son of good family from Jambudvīpa... [as detailed at length] ... has ascended to the third stage and desires to fight with Māra."
The faction of Māra is diminished;
the faction of the True Dharma is increased.
Having heard that from Śakra, the lord of the gods, [he said: (3.6) ...
The Yāma gods become even more delighted in mind.
(16) (4.1.1) Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk penetrate from the third stage-interval into the fourth stage-interval?
He sees, by means of knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye:
(4.1.2) he enters into the interior of the fourth stage:
"Conditioned by contact, a pleasant feeling has arisen for me—one whose cause is pleasure, whose source is pleasure, and whose condition is pleasure."
That [feeling] was ceased, stilled, and vanished.
Immediately following it, a painful feeling arose for me—unpleasant to touch, having suffering as its source, suffering as its origin, being indeed suffering, and conditioned by suffering.
Thus he recognizes feeling as having contact as its condition.
“From moment to moment, a feeling arises for me, accompanied by contact and originating from contact.
Toward that pleasant feeling, he does not rejoice, does not become impassioned;
he does not delight in that feeling, does not cultivate it, and does not relish it.”
In this way, even regarding painful feeling, he is not oppressed, not afflicted, and not disturbed.
He dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
When the mind becomes utterly dispassionate toward these three feelings, [it attains liberation].
Then, ultimately, only equanimity remains;
it becomes perfectly purified and perfectly cleansed. To him, it occurs thus:
“O, that I might apply this equanimity—
so pure, so cleansed—
to the sphere of infinite space!”

My mind would become conformable to that: equanimity has been realized by me, brought to its ultimate limit, firmly established, thoroughly resolved upon, and fully acquired. May I, therefore, apply this equanimity to the sphere of infinite space.
I too would apply this equanimity— so pure and so cleansed— to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
“Having thus attained and dwelt in this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, [he thinks]: ‘May my mind become conformable to that; may equanimity based upon it remain.’”
Because it is grasped by that, one identifies with it:
"May I, as such, bring about equanimity in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
(4.1.5) It is just as if a skilled smith or a smith’s apprentice were to place gold in the mouth of a forge.
Having cast [it] in, and having taken up the tube-seat-bite,
one should thus make this well-worked.

And that gold, being auspicious, beautiful, of excellent color, praiseworthy for its suitability for all types of work, refined according to the requirements of every region, present, with dross, stains, and impurities removed, soft, workable, and highly esteemed, envelops the gem with its luster. Then that skilled smith, or a smith’s apprentice, having recognized that the gold has been well-refined, [proceeds to fashion it].
In whatever modification of the binding he desires— whether for a bell, or for a pendant, or for an armlet, or for the beauty of the eyes, or for the beauty of a book,

or for the beauty of the hand, or for the beauty of the fingers, or for a finger-ring seal, or for a golden garland, or for the ornamentation of a crown— in whichever [place] he applies it, in that very place it becomes functional.
(4.1.6) In the same way, a monk who is well-trained in wisdom thinks: "I possess this equanimity, which is thus pure and thus cleansed."
If I were to apply myself to the sphere of infinite space, my mind would become conformable to that; equanimity would abide.
It is based upon that, bound to that, and determined by that, because of its grasping of that.
He applies that equanimity to the sphere of infinite space.
He applies [this] to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It occurs to him: "Would that this equanimity of mine were permanent, stable, eternal, and subject to no change?"
He, having realized reality, is one who has attained the fourth base:
"In the formless realms, my equanimity is neither permanent nor does it have a permanent object; it is neither stable nor does it have a stable object."
They are to be understood as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). They do not have the eternal as their object;

rather, they have the sphere of infinite space as their object, the sphere of infinite consciousness as their object, the sphere of nothingness as their object, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object.
This is characterized by equanimity;
this is auspicious; this is beneficial through equanimity.
(20) (4.1.7) Experiencing a feeling that has the body as its limit,
he recognizes it as it arises; he recognizes it as it ceases.
He recognizes the feeling born of eye-contact;
he recognizes the feeling born of ear-contact;
he recognizes the feeling born of nose-contact.
In this way, he recognizes the feeling born of contact with the tongue, body, and mind.
That monk, the witness of feelings, observes that very feeling in an even more subtle manner.
He experiences the feeling born of eye-contact as it arises, having arisen, and while it persists.
He recognizes that which has ceased and that which is ceasing: "My feeling has ceased.
(4.1.8.2) Furthermore, he recognizes another feeling born of auditory contact:
“That feeling of mine born of eye-contact has ceased, come to an end, been vomited out; it will not come again.”
When that [ear-consciousness] has ceased, this other feeling born of ear-contact arises— whether it has a pleasant object, a painful object, or an object that is neither pleasant nor painful.
As he contemplates and understands that feeling born of ear-contact exactly as it is,
he does not become attached to the feeling dependent upon the ear.
Experiencing that feeling, he becomes dispassionate and is liberated.
(4.1.8.3) When the feeling born of ear-contact has ceased, a feeling based on the nose arises. He experiences that feeling originating from the nose:
“A sensation born of nose-contact has arisen for me: one with a pleasant object is pleasant; one with a painful object is painful.”
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant is that which has neither-painful-nor-pleasant as its object. He experiences the feeling based on the nose as it truly is.
He also perceives its cessation.
When that has ceased, a feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises with the nose as its object;
he perceives that.
“For a sensation based on my nose will indeed arise;
just as it has arisen and been grasped,
so too will this which has arisen cease.”
(4.1.8.4–6) When that [feeling] has ceased, a threefold feeling based on the tongue will arise... as before... a threefold [feeling] based on mental feeling.
(4.1.9) He enters the fourth stage, which is truly existent and vastly expanded regarding feeling.

(4.1.10) When he has thus initiated vigor and possesses enthusiasm, desiring to break the bonds of Māra, the terrestrial yakṣas, being exceedingly joyful, announce it to the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere.
They, in turn, inform the Four Great Kings;
they, in turn, inform the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings;
and they, in turn, inform Śakra, the lord of the gods.
Śakra, too, announced it to the Yāma gods:
"That noble son from Jambudvīpa, from such-and-such a region and such-and-such a village, a noble son named so-and-so,
has shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron-colored robes."
Out of faith, he went forth from the household life into homelessness. Striving and exerting himself, he gradually ascended to the fourth stage, which is truly real and vast in its experience.
Therefore, O gods, I announce this to you:
the faction of Māra is being diminished;
the true faction of the gods and the True Dharma is being uplifted.
(4.1.11) Seeing Śakra mounted upon Airāvaṇa,
the Yāma gods were delighted and announced it to Śakra: “It is pleasing to us, O Śakra.”
"Just as the humans of Jambudvīpa are righteous and followers of the Dharma,
so too, Śakra, are you a mere semblance of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
How does that monk, while abandoning and thoroughly relinquishing the bonds of Māra,
observe feeling?
With knowledge derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
(4.2.2) That monk observes feeling as it truly is:
"An unwholesome [feeling] has arisen, having eye-consciousness as its object. As it was arising, it was ceased by means of a second, wholesome object."
It has become wholesome.
By means of an indeterminate object, it has been ceased and has become indeterminate.
"In the same way, feeling born of ear-contact, [feeling born of] nose-contact... (23)
He experiences feeling born of contact: feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
As he experiences them, wholesome qualities reach fulfillment, and his afflictions become attenuated.
(4.2.3) For one who cultivates it in this way, he examines that very feeling with subtle discernment.
He sees the feeling of mental phenomena ceasing along with another feeling of mental phenomena.
Just as the light of a lamp is opposed by the light of the sun,
so too is this pair of sensations ceased.
Furthermore, one experiences the wholesome and unwholesome sensations as they are being nourished.
Just as the light of one lamp nourishes a second lamp’s light,
he further analyzes feeling:
"Which feeling is absolutely opposed to which other feeling?"
He sees: "Wholesome feeling is absolutely opposed to unwholesome feeling;
just as the light of a lamp is opposed to the light of the stars.
(4.2.6) Furthermore, that monk analyzes further:
“What kind of feeling utterly destroys another feeling?
He sees: “A feeling that has the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as its object utterly destroys a feeling that has the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as its object;
just as the radiance of fire destroys the radiance of frost.”
(24) (4.2.7) “Which feeling, overcome by which feeling, is replenished once again?
He sees: “When an unwholesome feeling overcomes a wholesome feeling, that [unwholesome feeling] is replenished once again.”
Just as the light of the moon is eclipsed by the sun during the day, yet that same lunar light increases at night;
(4.2.8) furthermore, that monk, with mindfulness one-pointedly focused on feeling, analyzes feelings:
“Which many sensations, when combined, are overcome by which single sensation that is opposed to them?
He sees: “Many worldly sensations are overcome by the supramundane, untainted sensation.
It is just as the many lights of the constellations, planets, and stars at night are overcome by the light of the moon alone.”
(4.2.9) Furthermore, that monk, observing feelings and observing their exhaustion and disappearance, examines feelings even more subtly:
"How many are the numerous feelings arising from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and what wholesome [qualities] do they initiate?
He sees: "Though worldly feelings with outflows are numerous, they are not capable of perceiving the state without outflows."
Just as at night the radiance of the constellations, planets, and stars becomes incapable of being seen due to the absence of the moon;
(25) (4.2.10) furthermore, that monk examines that feeling:
"For how long a duration do my feelings persist?"
He sees: “My feelings abide for only a moment of arising and passing away, just like lightning.
(4.2.11) Furthermore, that monk reflects in this way:
“Does visual sensation provide a share for olfactory sensation?
He sees: “Sensation has as its object the distinct faculties from the time of the bubble [of the embryo] onwards; it belongs to all the faculties.
Just as there is no single cause for those of different species, such as cows, horses, camels, donkeys, and buffaloes.”
In the same way, there is no single object for the five sense-faculties that have arisen from beginningless time and are established by nature.
Due to the difference in their objects, the sense-faculties have distinct objects,
just as [the species] cow, horse, camel, donkey, buffalo, and boar [are distinct].
(4.2.12) For that monk who thus contemplates feelings, a subtler knowledge arises.
He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that knowledge.
(4.2.13) As he so cultivates it—contemplating feelings and contemplating their exhaustion and disappearance—it occurs to him:
“From where do my feelings arising from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind come as they arrive?
Or, when ceasing, where do they go to accumulate? (26) (4.2.14) As that monk, observing the exhaustion and passing away of feelings, reflects while proceeding on the path, it occurs to him:
“Furthermore, visual sensation does not come from anywhere when it arises, nor does it go to any accumulation when it ceases.
Thus, visual sensation comes into being having previously not existed.”
Having come into being, it passes away;
visual sensation does not come from the eye, just as water does not come from the ocean’s depths.
When it ceases, it does not go to any accumulation anywhere,
just as rivers flowing downward follow toward the ocean;
thus, visual sensation comes into being having previously not existed.
Having come into being, they pass away.
Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these sensations are dependently originated.
(4.2.15) “It is just as when a skilled potter or a potter’s apprentice, depending upon a wheel, [fashions a vessel].”
Dependent upon a lump of clay, dependent upon exertion,
and dependent upon water,
A jar arises having a lump of clay as its cause. In that process, the jar does not come from anywhere as its source; nor, when ceasing, does it go to any place of accumulation.
Thus, the jar is arisen through causes and conditions.
Likewise, my eye arises depending on form, depending on light, and depending on space.
Dependent upon attention,
visual sensation arises—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Just as, if the causes and conditions for a jar are excellent,
the production of that very excellent jar occurs; but if they are not excellent, [the opposite follows].
In that case, the jar becomes beautiful;
in the very same way, if the causes, conditions, and objects of perception are beautiful, [the result will be so].
From that, beautiful sensations such as sight and so forth arise—
wholesome, accompanied by the true Dharma, and leading progressively toward Nirvana.
Just as beautiful [feelings] arise from causes, conditions, and objects that are beautiful, so too do unwholesome feelings of the eye and other senses arise;
these have passion, hatred, and delusion as their objects and lead to rebirth in saṃsāra, the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal kingdom.
(4.2.16) A monk whose consciousness is bound to the skillfulness regarding the fruits of all actions, while investigating sensation,
does not perceive sensation as dependent on a single thing,
nor as presided over by an agent.
Nor is it produced by a cause, nor is it accidental, nor is it immutable.
not eternal, not stable, not everlasting,
It is not of a nature that does not undergo transformation.
For one who perceives that aggregate of feeling, the craving for rebirth—
which is accompanied by delight and passion and is defiling— is abandoned.
(4.2.17) That monk who contemplates the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices the path.
As he thus cultivates it, his fetters are abandoned.
The underlying tendencies are vomited out.
(4.2.18) What are the fetters? They are as follows: the fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance, and the fetter of views. (28)
The fetter of grasping, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice—
these fetters are abandoned.
(4.2.19) Which underlying tendencies are vomited out?

They are as follows: the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), the latent tendency of desire for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*), the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), and the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*).

These, according to their predominance, cause one to revolve through the three states of existence, to wander among the three realms, to revolve through the three afflictions, to follow after the three times, to possess the three poisons, to experience the three types of feeling, to revolve through the three births, and become the cause of *saṃsāra*.
(4.2.20) Furthermore, that practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk understand the eye thus, together with its causes and conditions? Of what is the eye conditioned?
What is its cause, what is its source?
He perceives, by means of knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye:
the eye has karma as its cause.
Birth is brought about by karma,
just as a tree arises from a banyan seed. From that tree, in turn, a banyan seed is produced, which grows through causes and conditions.
In this very way, through ignorance, karma is brought about;
through karma, birth is brought about.
When there is birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair arise.
Thus, this entire ocean of foolish ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) is bound by the fetters of craving for the cause of karma;
it revolves like a wheel.
This is the reason.
This is the condition for all feelings and for perceptions.
Karma is not performed;
due to the absence of karma, there is also the absence of craving.
Due to the absence of that, there is the absence of sensation.
From causes and conditions. (4.2.22) For example: depending upon the wick, and...
Dependent upon the vessel, dependent upon the oil,
and dependent upon the fire,
The flames of a lamp arise momentarily;

in the very same way, that monk, perceiving the causes and conditions of sensation and seeking reality, [sees that]: "All sensations arise born from the cause of karma, having karma as their refuge, and originating from karma."
That vessel is the body in such a state;
the sense-faculties are the oil, craving is the wick,
and passion, hatred, and delusion are the fire.
Momentary is cognition, like the flame of a lamp.
Like the radiance [of that flame] is the cognition by which the practitioner of yoga seeking reality perceives:
"All sensations contained within the three realms of existence."
(4.2.23) It is just as a goldsmith, having taken gold that is workable and fit for work, takes that gold and fashions it into a beautiful variety of ornaments.
In the same way, the practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) is like a goldsmith;
taking up an object of focus that resembles gold, if it is a beautiful object, [he refines it].
It brings about beautiful karma that leads to nirvāṇa.
Just as the object of focus is beautiful,
so too does it bring about beautiful karma.
And there are verses on this subject:
Knowing the reality of causes and conditions, having reached certainty regarding subtle matters,
and delighting in the stream of liberation, one is never carried away by craving.
(4.2.24.1) (30) All embodied beings rely upon karma; born from the womb of karma, they are bound to the fruit by karma and wander through the perils of existence.
He who does not take up unwholesome action and is always devoted to wholesome action,
such a yogi becomes one whose delight is as pure as the rays of the moon.
(4.2.24.3) Consuming evil states as fire consumes dry fuel,
he shines forth in the three worlds, freed from sin and having conquered all affliction.
But he whose mind is not at all inclined toward cyclic existence for the sake of liberation is not bound in saṃsāra; he is liberated like a bird in the sky.
(4.2.24.5) One who knows the reality of the arising of sensation and has certainty regarding the fruit of sensation—
he should be known as "liberated," for he is a knower of the truth of the three realms of existence.
(4.2.24.6) (31) He whom neither pleasure nor pain afflict, who is not stained by what is seen or unseen,
and who beholds cyclic existence as ablaze— he is considered a yogi by the virtuous.
One whose mind is never deluded, who is constantly devoted to the Dharma,
and who delights in the conduct of a mendicant— such a person is a true bhikṣu.
(4.2.24.8) One who finds no delight in seeing kinsmen, but delights in seeing the virtuous, and who has departed from the defilements of the household— that kind of person is a true mendicant.
With all his faculties completely stilled and no longer greedy for sense objects,
such a monk gazes only as far as the distance of a yoke’s length before him.
One who wanders into houses where he is reviled, one who engages in buying and selling merchandise, and one who delights in market streets and crossroads— such a person is not a true mendicant.
(4.2.24.11) (32) He who does not look upon singing or dancing, nor takes delight in worldly distractions, but finds his joy in the cremation ground— such a one is a true bhikṣu.
He takes almsfood sufficient for at most one day and does not look forward to tomorrow;
content with filling two-thirds of his stomach, such is the monk.
He who avoids the finest garments and delights in rag-robes, and who is disciplined in diet and conduct— such a one is a true bhikṣu.
He who does not undertake actions, who is free from expectations regarding all deeds,
who is without longing and has not entered [the worldly life]— such a person is a true mendicant.
(4.2.24.15) (33) One who is completely freed from desire and anger, who has abandoned the mire of delusion,
and who is not smeared by sinful qualities— such a person is a true bhikṣu.
Transcending all fetters, free from all latent tendencies,
and liberated from all underlying inclinations— such is the monk.
Standing before the city of Nirvana by means of the Noble Eightfold Path,
such a monk disperses all afflictions.
With senses stilled, firm in intellect, and free from the mire of desire,
with a mind established in one-pointed concentration— such is the monk.
He who knows the transition between the stages and perceives the true nature of those stages.
Such is the monk who knows the higher and lower stages of the path.
(4.2.24.20) (34) Such a monk is one who knows, according to the rule, all phenomena— both those with outflows and those without outflows— as arising from causes and conditions.
A celibate student who is upright, tranquil, and free from sloth and torpor;
who rises at the proper time, pure and skillful—such a one becomes a true mendicant.
One who delights in tranquility and insight, who delights in the four meditative absorptions,
and who finds joy in the forest— such a one is a monk.
Like the shadow of a bird in flight that always follows it, so too does his mind ever follow the true Dharma; such a one is a true bhikṣu.

(4.2.24.24) Such is the monk who destroys the afflictions and secondary afflictions, who perceives that [reality], possesses pure intelligence, and is skilled in the method of mindfulness of breathing.

(4.2.24.25) (35) A monk who knows the sequence of the rules, who is a knower of yoga, a seer of reality, and who knows the method of what is the path and what is not the path— such a one is a [true] monk.
(4.2.24.26) He who does not rejoice in delights and does not fear in the face of fears— one who is equanimous toward joy and fear, such a hero becomes a true mendicant.
One who knows the reality of old age and death, who is honored by gods and asuras,
and who knows the higher and the lower among beings— such a person becomes a monk.
Content with the outer robe and the alms bowl, he does not delight in accumulations;
such is the monk who has few desires and lives the holy life.
Eating at a single sitting, pure, and not deluded by greed for flavors— one who is detached from gain and honor is such a bhikṣu.

(4.2.24.30) (36) Delighting in equanimity and compassion, free from the fault of concealment, with all his defilements utterly consumed— such is the monk. (4.2.24.31) (4.2.25) That monk, contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena, observes that very feeling as it truly is.
With subtler knowledge, he sees that the feeling born of eye-contact follows after its object;
he sees it ceasing along with a second object and being destroyed: "The feeling born of eye-contact, having its object, has passed away."
"A feeling—whether desirable or undesirable—has arisen for me accompanied by sound as its object;
may my mind, accompanied by that [feeling], not fall into transformation.
Having fixed that mind upon the pillar of the object, he...
He maintains [his attention].

When that auditory sensation, which was accompanied by the objective support of sound, has ceased, an olfactory sensation with fragrance as its objective support arises. He observes and reflects upon that olfactory sensation as well:
“A nose-consciousness accompanied by odor has arisen for me,
whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate;
my mind has become distorted toward that nose-consciousness.”
When he observes a transformation of the mind,
he again fixes upon that very same object of focus; he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort.
He makes the mind pliable and cultivates it with wholesome, untainted dharmas;
then it does not waver.
He takes as his object of focus that which pertains to the tongue—
whether wholesome, unwholesome, determinate, or indeterminate— and at that time, having directly realized that object of focus, he...
He observes feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant: "Why has my mind fallen into a state of distortion because of this? he asks himself.
“If he sees that the mind has fallen into a state of distortion when a feeling based on taste has arisen,
he again binds that very mind to the pillar of the object with the rope of fortitude;
he thus conducts himself, exerts himself, and strives in such a way that his mind is not carried away by the thirst for taste associated with the sensation of the tongue.”

Furthermore, that monk, having bound the tactile sensation associated with the body's tangible objects to the pillar of the focal object, examines it as wholesome, unwholesome, determinate, or indeterminate.
If he observes that his mind has fallen into a state of distortion due to that tactile sensation,
he binds it once more to the pillar of that very object and makes it pliant so that it does not fall into distortion again.
Furthermore, that monk observes the mental sensations associated with the mind— whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, determinate, or indeterminate.
If he allows those sensations to cause a distortion of the mind, [he recognizes it].
Having bound that object with the rope of steadfastness,
he makes it workable so that it does not undergo any distortion.
(38) (4.2.26) He observes the feeling pertaining to the body within the six sense objects.
The monk ascends to the state known as the vision of the arising of the reality of the five feelings.
(4.2.27.1) He examines with the lamp of knowledge the feeling born of eye-contact:
"Who experiences this feeling?"
‘This is feeling’?
(4.2.27.2) He sees: “Dependent upon mental consciousness, ...”
This feeling that has arisen is bound to the mind and is carried away by mental discursive thought.
All foolish ordinary people are burned by the fire of conceptualization;
herein there is no agent nor any experiencer.
It is merely an aggregate of formations that arises;
it is merely an aggregate of formations that ceases, bound by causes and conditions.
“Observing the feeling born of eye-contact as it truly is, and following after it,
he is not carried away by it;
his mind does not waver, is not made hollow, and is not made turbid.”
(4.2.27.3) Furthermore, that monk contemplates auditory sensation:
"Who is this that experiences auditory sensation, thinking, 'This is a sensation,' and feels it? (39)
(4.2.27.4) He sees: "This auditory sensation is bound up with mental consciousness; it is bound to the mind and dependent upon it."
Here there is neither an agent nor an experiencer;
this auditory sensation is dependently originated. Here there could be neither an agent nor an experiencer.
“This heap of conditioned formations is empty; having arisen by the power of causes and conditions, it ceases.
(4.2.27.5) Furthermore, that monk observes olfactory sensation:
“Who is it that experiences this sensation?”
‘This is feeling’? (4.2.27.6) He sees: “Feeling is bound up with mental consciousness.”

Having that as its object, depending upon it, caused by it, and conditioned by it, there arises an experience characterized by [the realization]: "This heap of formations is empty; it is not presided over by an agent, nor is it presided over by an experiencer;
it proceeds as a continuous succession.
Having observed the sensation of the nose...
“Here there is no agent or experiencer as a separate entity.
(4.2.27.7) Furthermore, that monk contemplates the sensation of the tongue:
“Who is it that experiences this sensation of the tongue?”
‘This is a tongue-feeling’?
(4.2.27.8) He sees: “This tongue-feeling is bound up with mental consciousness.”
It arises depending on that, bound to that, having that as its object, and originating from that as its cause; it has that as its basis.
Herein, there is no agent or experiencer existing as a separate entity.
“This heap of conditioned forces is empty; it arises by the power of causes and conditions.
(40) (4.2.27.9) Furthermore, that monk examines the sensation of touch in the body:
“Who is this that experiences the bodily sensation?”
Regarding the phrase "in feeling" (vedanāyām):
he sees that "this bodily feeling is bound up with mental consciousness."
"Herein, there is no agent or experiencer existing as a separate entity.
This empty aggregate of formations proceeds by the power of causes and conditions.
(4.2.27.11) Furthermore, that monk observes mental feeling:
“Who experiences mental feeling [thinking]: ‘This is a mental feeling’?
“Dependent upon the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. From the coming together of these three, contact occurs; and feeling is co-nascent with contact.”
For example: from a collection of many fragrant substances, a beautiful fragrance arises.
And for that fragrance, there is no single cause of its existence. In the same way, all sensations arise from a collection of causes and conditions.
They are not presided over by an agent, nor are they presided over by an experiencer.
(4.2.28) “For example, depending upon the leaf and depending upon the filament, ...”
Dependent upon the stalk and dependent upon the filaments,
the flower called a lotus arises.
And for that lotus, no single cause is found;
likewise, depending upon the eye, depending upon the object, depending upon space, and depending upon mental attention, [it arises].
And depending upon light, feeling born of eye-contact arises.

This feeling, which belongs to the category of the eye and is supported by the eye, is not of a single kind; it consists of many substances, arises from many sources, is neither immutable nor created.
(4.2.29) Just as the mendicant becomes a seeker of reality to whatever extent, so to that same extent do his bright qualities manifest.
It is just like sugarcane juice collected in a vessel and boiled over a fire.
Its first impurity becomes liquid, known as *phāṇita*;
the second is turbid molasses; the third is a decoction known as *guḍa*, which becomes whiter, and the fourth becomes even whiter.
Just as sugarcane juice becomes increasingly clearer the more it is boiled,
even so, the sugarcane juice of the mental continuum— being heated by the fire of wisdom within the vessel of the focal object— is brought to a boil.
His attainment of the first dhyāna is like molasses;
his attainment of the second dhyāna is whiter still, like jaggery;
his attainment of the third dhyāna is like granulated sugar.
In this very way, just as a monk boils the continuum of the mind with the fire of knowledge,
so too do the untainted dharmas arise— whiter, more stainless, and more free from defilement;
they arise turned away from saṃsāra, white, free from impurity, and cleansed.
(4.2.30) Furthermore, that monk observes that feeling in another way as even more subtle:
"A subtle and coarse feeling, born of eye-contact, defiled and accompanied by delusion, has arisen in such-and-such a being;
it is afflicted by that other coarse feeling."
It was made to subside with a remainder.
In the same way, auditory sensation, olfactory sensation, gustatory sensation, tactile sensation, and mental sensation [were treated].
(42) (4.2.31) As that monk was thus striving and exerting himself, dispersing the army of Māra, the terrestrial yakṣas, with minds exceedingly joyful, [informed] the celestial yakṣas...
They announce it.
Those terrestrial yakṣas and the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere announce it to the four Great Kings.
Those terrestrial yakṣas, those yakṣas who roam the atmosphere, and those four Great Kings announce it to the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings.
Those terrestrial yakṣas,
those yakṣas who roam the atmosphere, those four Great Kings, and those gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings inform Śakra:
"This Śakra, the lord of the Thirty-three and king of the gods, having mounted Airāvaṇa,"
With a most joyful mind, he reports [this] to the Yāma gods... as before... (4.2.32).

Those Yāma gods, too, being pleased by Śakra, possess various colored jewels; their bodies are adorned with divine garlands and perfumes; they have various pleasures and desired sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells; and being free from the suffering of comparison, they are exceedingly delighted and hasten toward the gods.

The sections: Among the Tuṣita gods, there is a city named Mānasasaṅkalpa, forty thousand yojanas in extent, illuminated by palaces made of the seven precious gems and containing various celestial mansions.
Therein is the street of the Bodhisattvas, ten thousand yojanas long, known as Nirāsravarati.
In that city dwells the Blessed One Maitreya together with five hundred closely associated bodhisattvas.

And when his mind is exceedingly joyful, the Yāma gods inform him, prostrating themselves on the ground with their kneecaps, arranging divine garments over one shoulder, and placing their joined palms upon their heads, saying: "O Lord,..."

From Jambudvīpa, the locus of the land of karma— from such-and-such a village, such-and-such a district, such-and-such a town, and such-and-such a family— a certain son of good family has shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of faith has gone forth from the home to the homeless life.
Practicing, striving, and attending upon his teachers,

seeking the reality of the untainted virtues, he ascends to the fourth stage, called "The Vision of the Reality of Feeling," where he shatters the faction of Māra and strengthens the bridge of the True Dharma.
He illuminates the white dharmas;
the faction of Māra becomes weakened,
while the faction of the gods becomes strengthened.
“We inform the gods of this.
(4.2.33) Having heard that from the presence of the Yāma gods, Maitreya [thought],
“The side of the gods is gaining strength.”
He spoke thus: "I am delighted,
O gods."
The faction of Māra is diminished, the faction of the True Dharma is increased,
and the afflictions are rendered lax.
The army of Māra is put to flight.
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk, having seen the six groups of feeling as they truly are, [perceive them] in brief by way of the stage of the aggregate of feeling?
Does he ascend to the fifth intermediate stage?

(44) (5.1.2) Furthermore, that monk, perceiving the reality of sensation and having brought his activities to an end through the six bodies of sensation, thoroughly analyzes and characterizes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): "Which intermediate stage is this one, accompanied by perception, who—practicing in seclusion from white dharmas—is reflecting upon?"
“Could one who moves about discerning between the beneficial and the harmful be a perceiver of perception?
(5.1.3) He takes up the signs of wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*).
From the very beginning, he analyzes phenomena (*dharma*).
“How is it that the perception of the non-visible and the non-obstructive arises for those things that have as their objects the visible and the obstructive?
He contemplates that perception as being more secluded;
by means of that perception, he takes as his object the sign of the eleven kinds of form.
Namely: long, short, square, circular, triangular, blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson.
(5.1.4.1) Therein, one forms a sign of perception regarding length: "Alas, the cycle of existence for fools of dull intellect is long, without beginning or end."

This [saṃsāra] is composed of birth, death, the fruits of karma, passing away and rebirth, separation from the beloved, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, fatigue, exhaustion, being sent into service by others, humiliation, the state of slavery, and mutual devouring; it is the locus of all misfortunes, immeasurable and unbearable.

Fools and ordinary worldlings have been repeatedly and repeatedly mocked and adorned with specific karmic deeds—difficult to perform—that arise from body, speech, and mind, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.

(45) (5.1.4.2) “In that regard, for those who have become human beings, this saṃsāra is long for those whose minds are preoccupied with the pursuit [of wealth], addiction, deceiving others, fraudulent measures, commerce, service to royal courts, voyages to the ocean, exile, strife, agriculture, animal husbandry, birth among barbarians, wrong views, being deficient in sense faculties, separation from the true Dharma, lack of the conditions for the arising of a Buddha, the unfavorable states (*akṣaṇa*), drinking intoxicants, taking what is not given, false speech, sexual misconduct, covetousness, malice, and idle chatter.
“He grasps at the sign of perception:
‘Long is the cycle of existence for the gods,’ and he grasps at the sign of perception.”

“For those gods whose minds are attached to sense objects—addicted to desired sounds, tastes, touches, smells, passion, hatred, delusion, and negligence; addicted to the vices of women and to the Pārijātaka tree, the Caitraratha grove, pleasure gardens, ponds, lotus-pools, play-grounds, perfumes, flowers, the essence of nectar, various games, food, and diversions; addicted to sandalwood, divine garlands, powders, ointments, Māndārava flowers, divine music, and the songs of gandharvas; and who are turned away from the True Dharma—their saṃsāra is long.
(5.1.4.4) For the hungry ghosts (*pretas*) as well, the saṃsāra is long, as they cling to the signs of perception (*sañjñā-nimitta*).

“[The sufferings] of those who go to the realm of ill-performed karma: hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and weakness; being scorched by fire and drenched by rain; falling [into pits]; having throats as narrow as needles and bellies like mountains; being born as *kabhallika* insects; mutual envy and malice; being cut to pieces by one another with weapons; falling into dark, abyssal chasms; being swept away by rivers, ponds, and lakes; being struck by the blows of the swords, staves, and spades of Yama’s messengers; and eating vomit and spittle.”

Their faces and limbs were covered with hair that had become like a dark storm-cloud from the falling of tears born of various unbearable sufferings and hunger arising over many hundreds of thousands of years; their bodies were infested by hundreds of thousands of worms and had become the seat of a multitude of all diseases.

Carrying such forms, they had entered into the long cycle of saṃsāra; their eyes were gouged out by iron crows with flaming beaks, and they resembled trees burnt by a forest fire as they were attacked by others and by one another.

For those hungry ghosts (*preta*) who are being devoured, who have entered a wilderness extending for thirty-six million *yojanas*, who are helpless, whose bodies are scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, who are sinking in darkness, who are averse to hearing the True Dharma, and who are deceived by false views— the long cycle of saṃsāra is perceived as a sign of conceptualization.

(5.1.4.5) “There are aquatic creatures—such as dolphins, hunters, mongooses, whales, *timiṅgila* fish, crocodiles, sharks, makaras, oysters, conchs, and others—who are averse to knowledge regarding mutual devouring and forbidden sexual conduct; who are constantly afflicted by thirst; who fear being seized with their hearts parched; who are perpetually intent on devouring one another, both large and small;
and who dread being caught and cast down into nets.”
Likewise, [he saw] those who move on land— such as deer, buffalo, boars, elephant kings, bulls, horses, donkeys, gayals, ruru deer, bears, and gaṇḍaka antelopes—
and others afflicted by hundreds of thousands of various sufferings, such as bondage, weapons, slaughter, disease, old age, death, and mutual torment;

and likewise those who move in the air— such as crows, owls, swans, peacocks, cocks, quails, pigeons, dātyūha cranes, vāsas, śatapattras, chāyāvalīnas, jīvajīvaka birds, cuckoos, and other [creatures].
And for the species of birds and animals—

those dwelling in the three realms, moving on land, in water, or through the air, belonging to the animal realm, and tormented by slaughter, binding, weapons, hunger, thirst, mutual devouring, cold, and heat—
their long cycle of saṃsāra is harsh and terrifying.

“He takes the sign of perception as his object. (5.1.4.6) Likewise, [he perceives those] in the Sañjīvana, Kālasūtra, Saṅghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci hells, along with their elevated regions—those who are afflicted by various kinds of unbearable causes of suffering, such as the falling of fires and weapons of hundreds of thousands of fearsome types that are most difficult to conceive; the Vaitaraṇī river of blood; the melting of limbs and members; the entry into sword-leaves; the experiencing of glowing coals; the falling into the caustic river; the crossing of the blazing ground; and the inexhaustible smoke and fire resembling harsh sand.”
The saṃsāra of those in hell is long;
he takes up the sign of perception as his object.

(5.1.4.7) That monk, while investigating the aggregate of perception, [perceives] long form that is visible and resistant—[namely] the four truths which have as their object the causes and conditions of the results of karma—for hundreds of thousands of various kinds of yojanas.
Furthermore, he observes sentient beings who have gone their various ways; he discerns them and analyzes them.
He perceives the causal basis as illuminated by the lamp of perception.
And he becomes weary of cyclic existence.
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk analyze and realize the short [vowels]?
With knowledge consisting of what has been heard or with the divine eye, he sees: how does that monk, putting Māra’s army to flight, analyze the short?

(5.1.5.2) “For those who delight in vows, restraints, giving, morality, knowledge, proper conduct, service to gurus, honesty, and a mind that is pleasing; for those who possess right view, reverence for mother and father, and the seeing and hearing of the Buddha and Dharma, as well as attendance upon teachers;

for those who abstain from deceitful behavior, false measures, and fraud; and for those humans whose bodies, speech, and minds are adorned by the character of spiritual friends, by honesty, a straightforward mind, and lack of miserliness—their cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is short.
Thus he apprehends the sign of perception.

(5.1.5.3) "Likewise, when negligence has arisen, those who— having disregarded the various excellent foods found in the Nandana, Vaibhrāja, Caitraratha, and Pārijātaka groves, as well as the ponds, lotus-pools, diverse sandalwood necklaces, offerings, and the splendors of the wish-fulfilling trees, rivers, springs, and forests; and who, instead,

find their various foods and pastimes in meditation, study, the sight of the virtuous, recitation, giving, self-restraint, discipline, celibacy, tranquility of the senses, moderation in speech, and a peaceful devotion to the Dharma through their food and conduct."
“O gods, for those [beings], saṃsāra is short.

(49) (5.1.5.4) “As it has been described, those whose faces and so forth are withered by various sufferings such as hunger and thirst, and whose bodies resemble trees burnt by a forest fire— with their hair and faces licked by the flames of that conflagration— ”
Disregarding even a painful death,
those whose faculties are clear for even a moment and who have brief but genuine faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—
for them, cyclic existence is short.
“They grasp at the signs of perception:
(5.1.5.5) those who are terrified by the fear of mutual devouring, threatening, beating, cold, heat, foul weather, and so forth—
if they are able— ”
If, disregarding even a moment’s obstruction,
they can produce a single moment of serene confidence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
their wandering in the animal realm will be short.
“He grasps at the sign of perception:

those who have been reborn in hells such as Sañjīvana, Kālasūtra, Saṅghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci, and who are afflicted by various transformations and supreme sufferings—
disregarding that suffering [he grasps at the sign].”
Those who clarify their minds for even a moment regarding ethical discipline—
their existence in the hells as hell-beings will be short;
they do not grasp at the signs of perception.
He thus reflects upon the brevity of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
For whom is cyclic existence square?
He sees: "For the men of Uttarakuru—who are free from possessiveness and egoism and are destined for an upward course—cyclic existence is square among them."
“He grasps at the signs of perception.

(50) (5.1.7) For those in the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—who revolve through ignorance and do not follow their own true mind—the cycle of existence is circular; he grasps at the signs of perception.”

(5.1.8) “Regarding those who have performed pure, impure, indeterminate, or mixed karma, and who are born among humans with a mixture of hellish and celestial results— therein, by impure karma they go to the hells,
by pure karma they go to the heavens, and by mixed karma they go among humans. Those who are subject to the three types of karma are those born in the three states of existence.”
Among them, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is triangular;
it pursues the signs of perception (*saṃjñā-nimitta*).

(5.1.9) Those belonging to the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, and those born according to their karma among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, having passed away from the gods, are reborn among the gods.
For those who, having passed away from among humans, are reborn again among humans and not in the states of no opportunity (akṣaṇabhūmi),
their cyclic existence (saṃsāra) is a circle;
they grasp at the signs of perception (saṃjñānimitta).
(51) (5.1.10) “The denizens of hell are gripped by dark and unwholesome karma; for they sink into hells consisting of darkness,
and they grasp at the signs of perception.”
(5.1.11) “The hungry ghosts (*preta*) are comprised of yellow-colored karma.
For those hungry ghosts are intent upon mutual malice, beating, and threatening; they perceive the sign of their own designation.”
(5.1.12) "Animals are comprised within the karma of blood;
for they delight in mutual devouring and blood.
One perceives the sign of the perception."
(5.1.13) “Devas and humans, indeed, encompassed by white-colored karma, acquire rebirth among gods and humans through the price of wholesome and auspicious paths of action consisting of jewels.
When a god is about to pass away, other gods say:
‘Go to a happy destination, to the world of humans.’”
Likewise, as he is dying, his kinsmen, friends, and wives, their faces clouded by the rain of tears in their eyes, say:
"To a happy rebirth in the world of men!"
"Dear one, go, leaving us behind;
you perceive the sign of perception."
(5.1.14) He reflects thus:
"Having attained this human state,
he who does not strive for the sake of wholesome generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom,"
Deceived and accumulated by the paths of karma, that foolish ordinary person wanders through the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

(5.1.15) That monk, seeing the reality of feeling, sees the reality of the object of appropriate mental attention regarding the aggregate of perception; he seeks only the truth: (52) (5.1.16) "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises."
Contact is the coming together of the three.
Therein, he analyzes perception (*saṃjñā*):
form seen as beautiful or ugly, near or far, long or short, square, circular, white, triangular, and the configuration of form (*rūpasaṃsthāna*).
He analyzes perception, forms mental signs, and examines the causal basis.
He perceives and analyzes the causal basis of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
He bears witness to the detailed classification of the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
One relies upon that which is endowed with reason;
having understood that which is devoid of reason,
one abandons it.

He causes one to perceive that which is beneficial, that which is harmful, and that which is distinct from both, as well as the past (*atīta*)—[this is difficult... [as before... ...he causes one to perceive within perception itself:
"If perception did not exist..."
Even memory would not exist;
for that memory is bound to perception, having that as its objective support and that as its causal condition.
Just as the light of a lamp has the lamp as its condition,
originating from it and having it as its cause,
even so my mindfulness has perception as its cause, originates from perception, and has perception as its dominant influence.
That monk ascends to the fifth intermediate stage, which is called the contact of perception (*saṃjñā-sparśa*).
He perceives the happiness of the gods there as it truly is, yet he does not rejoice in it.
He does not even fear the suffering caused by karma for those in the hells.
(53) (5.1.17) That monk, who views all things with equanimity and perceives them as being like refined gold, observes that very perception in another way:
he observes another person, freed from such perceptions, who has died.
“What is the condition for this perception of mine? What is its cause, what is its source?
He sees: “This perception of mine is dependently originated; it arises solely through the assembly of conditions.”
Through the cessation of that, it ceases.
(54) (5.1.18) “Just as, depending upon the moon and depending upon the moonstone (*candrakāntamaṇi*), [water flows forth]...”
Just as clear water appears from a moonstone,
even so, perception is produced in dependence upon causes and conditions.
This perception is not without cause;
it is not made by an agent,
nor by an experiencer.
It does not arise by chance.
(5.1.19) He, as a monk in truth, investigates the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
He is one who perceives the reality of perception.
He, knowing the reality of arising and passing away and investigating the most subtle sequence,

perceives that while a wholesome state arises with the designation of a river’s current flowing along its bank, it undergoes transformation into an unwholesome state by the power of conditions and causes.
An unwholesome state, while arising, is transformed into wholesomeness by the power of its conditions and causes;
yet once born, it is again struck down by the monkey of the mind.
They have arisen as indeterminate;
they regard transformation as pleasure;
they perceive the notion of pleasure in the outflows-free pleasures.
And regarding pleasure, there is non-perception:

"In that very pleasure, there are limited perceptions" (5.1.20). How is it that one who perceives the cessation and arising of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the wholesome does not become attached to feeling?
He does not delight in the subsiding of feeling;
he does not take pleasure in the arising of perceptions through the subsiding of feeling,
nor in their persistence, nor in their passing away, nor in their alteration.
He does not delight in the arising of consciousness,
nor in its staying, nor in its destruction, nor in its transformation.
Thus, this monk who knows the reality of the aggregates does not dwell within the domain of Māra;
he is not afflicted by passion, hatred, and delusion,
nor does he come to view things as permanent, pleasurable, pure, or as a self.
He is not bound by the snares consisting of desirable sounds, touches, forms, smells, and tastes within the web-like cycle of existence;
he does not lose his mindfulness.
Possessing established mindfulness and discernment, he is capable of proceeding toward the destruction of the outflows and toward Nirvana.
And there are verses on this point:
A monk who does not constantly delight in exertion for the sake of seeing monks of weak vigor and indolent character is such a one.
(5.1.21.1) The Buddha has declared that a monk who shares his bed and seat [with others] is not a true mendicant;
he who delights in indolence does not deserve what is auspicious.
(5.1.21.2) (56) Laziness alone is indeed the root of all afflictions;
for whoever possesses laziness, no Dharma exists for them.
He who is called a "monk" merely by virtue of his robes alone [is such a person].
He whose mind is not set on study, nor on meditation, nor on the destruction of the outflows—
he is merely a semblance of a monk, existing through hypocrisy alone.
One who delights in monasteries and pleasure groves, but not in the sphere of the Dharma, whose mind is greedy for women and liquor— such a person would not be a true bhikṣu.
(5.1.21.5) He who cuts the bonds of Māra and cuts off evil karma— he is taught by the Buddhas to be a bhikṣu, not one who merely consumes food within the domain of the Saṅgha.
(5.1.21.6) (57) It would be better to consume the venom of a poisonous snake or even molten copper,
than to eat the food and drink belonging to the Sangha with those of immoral conduct.
For he who does not deserve alms is not fit for alms;
he whose afflictions have been consolidated is fit for hell.
He by whom the afflictions have been cast out like snakes from their holes—
that monk should subsist on alms-food and not be intent on looking at women.
If one makes oneself a captive and takes delight in evil deeds, how can such a person be known as a monk? He is a defiler of the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
He for whom gain and honor are the objects of his sacrifice,
who desires the sight of women and longs for them— he is neither a monk nor a householder, but a rogue.

(5.1.21.11) (58) Those by whom the forest of afflictions has been burned, like a forest consumed by fire—they are the twice-born, they are the auspicious ones; they are not attached to food and drink.
(5.1.21.12) Always eager to go to the village, always eager for bathing, these rogues are fools who deceive themselves and others; they are utterly deluded regarding the path of the true Dharma.
Those twice-born ones who, with minds ever tranquil in the forest, are constantly devoted to meditation— they are the virtuous ones, whose sphere of activity is the path of auspiciousness.
(5.1.21.14) Delightful are the forests, yet the mind finds no pleasure therein;
those free from passion will find delight here, but not those who seek after sensual desires.
But he who delights in idle talk and is addicted to craving for sense objects will not go to the peaceful city where death does not exist.
(5.1.21.16) One who serves kings, eats delicacies, drinks liquor, and is always wrathful deceives sincere donors under the name of a mendicant.
(5.1.21.17) For those who, having resorted to the king's gate by adopting a means of livelihood,
became embroiled with householders and fled to the forest for fear of destruction—

(5.1.21.18) Those who, having abandoned wife and children, have resorted to the peaceful forest, yet nourish their own well-being— such people are considered equal to those who eat what has been vomited. (5.1.21.19) (60) (5.1.22) That mendicant, having abandoned these faults...
Devoted to the vision of reality, perceiving the reality of the aggregates such as form, he strives and practices for the sake of liberation, and he questions his teacher.
Knowing the truth of what is the path and what is not the path, he seeks that city of liberation by means of the noble eightfold path.

One whose conduct is the undertaking of the path, who views all things with equanimity, whose mind is stainless and tranquil, cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that very path. For such a person,
who is joined with these wholesome and untainted paths of action, the faction of Māra diminishes and the faction of the True Dharma increases.
“Having understood this, the terrestrial yakṣas inform the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere;
they, in turn, inform the four Great Kings. (5.1.24)

Those four Great Kings... [as before] ... announce this to Maitreya while he is residing in Tuṣita; and the Yāma gods [do likewise]. Then, one Bodhisattva among the Tuṣitas, exceedingly intent on joy, announces it to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods: "A certain son of good family from Jambudvīpa has shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes... [as before] ..."; then the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, with minds even more delighted...
The gods: “... as before ... (61) (5.2.1).
Again, the practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk ascend to the fifth stage?
He sees with knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye:
(5.2.2) he beholds the ten material sense bases (*rūpy-āyatana*).
Which ten?

Namely: the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of visible forms, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of sounds, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of odors, the sense-base of the tongue, the sense-base of tastes, the sense-base of the body, and the sense-base of tangibles.
These are the material sense-bases.
(5.2.3.1) Here he observes: “How, depending upon my eye-base and depending upon the form-base, [does visual consciousness arise]?”
What perception arises?
He sees: "Dependent upon the eye... (5.2.3.2)
Dependent upon form, visual consciousness arises;
from the coming together of these three, contact occurs.
Feeling, perception, and volition are co-nascent with contact.
Therein, that which is feeling experiences;
that which is volition wills.
In that regard, whatever perception there is, it perceives thus:
"This form is long," or "This form is short."
"This form is pleasant;
this form is unpleasant;
this form is visible and possesses resistance."
‘This form is non-demonstrable and non-obstructive.
In this way, he analyzes the eleven types of form, up to that which is designated as non-informative (*avijñapti*).
(62) (5.2.3.3) Thus, from the coming together of the three, contact (*sparśa*) arises.
Feeling, perception, and volition are co-nascent with contact.
Among these, feeling, perception, and volition born of visual contact: the meaning of "feeling" (*vedanā*) is the sense of experiencing (*vindamāna*).
The meaning of "perception" (saññā) is the act of perceiving (sañjānanā).
For perception perceives the time of feeling (vedanā),
depending upon the mind (manas).
These phenomena arise with mutual characteristics and mutual natures;
