just as there are ten universal mental factors, the characteristic of volition is indeed distinct [from the others].

[These factors are] applied thought (*vitarka*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*saṃcetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
These have a single object but possess distinct characteristics from one another.
Thus, the characteristic of feeling is indeed different from the characteristic of perception.
For example: the rays of the sun have a single object, or else they are of different natures;
in the very same way, the nature of sensation is one thing, and the nature of volition is another.
(5.2.3.4) And he, knowing the reality of feeling, perception, and volition born of eye-contact, sees the eye itself as empty,
sees it as hollow, and sees it as devoid of essence.

A monk who sees reality as it is, who knows the truth of the path, and is free from false views, is preceded by right view; he abandons that very delusion associated with the eye, which is of a turbid nature,
by seeing the reality of the lump of flesh and thinking, "It is an abode of fat, pus, blood, and tears," and thus he abandons passion.
Thinking, "It is not eternal," one becomes a seer of its impermanence; thinking, "It is a mass of flesh," and "It is situated within the cavities of the bones," one becomes dispassionate.
Thinking, "It is bound by sinews," he understands, "This sense-base of the eye is mutually dependent;
there is no core substance here."
He realizes it is selfless;
understanding and seeing that, in brief, "this eye is of the nature of suffering," he perceives it.
One becomes dispassionate toward the sense-base of the eye.
(64) (5.2.3.5) Understanding the sense-base of the eye as it truly is, he also investigates visible forms:
“If that form—whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—is imagined as unreal, what essence is there in it?
What is pure? What is permanent? What is pleasant?”
“Seeing form, knowing it, and reflecting upon it, he gains this understanding:
‘There is no essence here in form;
this form, whether pleasant or unpleasant, is merely a product of conceptual construction.’”
"Here there is no state that is either pleasant or unpleasant;
it is only this world, seized by the conceptualizations of pleasure and anger, that thinks, 'It is pleasant' or 'It is hateful.
(5.2.4.1) Having observed the sphere of form with the eye, he...
He contemplates the sense-sphere of the ear and the sound; he examines that sound:
"A sound has arisen and falls within the range of the sense-faculty."
Then, depending upon the ear,
depending upon sound,
and depending upon the attention born thereof,
Auditory consciousness arises.
From the coming together of these three, contact occurs; born simultaneously with contact are feeling, perception, and volition.
Among these, that which intends, accompanied by perception, is feeling born simultaneous with contact.
For example: "This characteristic is long;
due to distance and from its cause, this sound has come about as a beautiful action—whether it be subtle, gross, pleasant, or unpleasant."
“He perceives the sound that has come, intends it, discerns it through perception, and cognizes it with mental consciousness.”
He feels through feeling;
he deliberates through doubt.
Clinging to the sense-base of the ear and sounds, he reflects.
Reflecting, he investigates;
investigating, he experiences:
"Here, by way of intrinsic nature, no sound exists as either pleasant or unpleasant."
This is merely a product of conceptual construction alone.
This sound is "pleasant" or "unpleasant"—this sound is not by its own nature eternal, or stable, or permanent, or happy, or substantial, or possessed of a self, or devoid of a self.
It is merely that passion, hatred, and delusion [arise] such that one thinks, "This sound is pleasant" or "This sound is unpleasant."
(5.2.4.2) While reflecting upon the sphere of the auditory faculty and its sounds,
having heard a sound,
he is neither deluded nor attached.
He does not understand passion.
Having thoroughly examined the sense base of the ear and sounds,
he does not become attached to auditory consciousness.
Nor does he approach passion [with the thought]:
"The ear-consciousness is not mine; the ear-consciousness is not my own."
“In the same way, contact, feeling, perception, and volition [are to be understood]. (5.2.5.1) Furthermore, that monk understands the sense-sphere of odors: ‘Dependent upon the nose, ...’”
Dependent upon odor and dependent upon the corresponding mental attention,
olfactory consciousness arises.
One smells what is near or distant, pleasant or unpleasant, fragrant or foul, that which is joined with or separated from the wind, and counter-odors.
In this regard, the sense-base of the nose and the external odor meet;
from the conjunction of these three arises contact, and born together with contact are feeling, perception, and among the formations, volition.
Therein, feeling has the characteristic of experiencing;
perception has the characteristic of perceiving;
and contact has the characteristic of internal touch, [arising] upon observing the sense base of the nose and odors.
Perception has the characteristic of perceiving through contact;
volition has the characteristic of mental formation.
These factors, though having a single moment as their object, initiate distinct functions.
That is to say, because they are mutually devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Just as the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*)... [as before] ...so too all these phenomena have distinct characteristics, and they do not initiate a single effect in a single moment.
(5.2.5.2) That monk, knowing the reality of the sense-field of odors, investigates it according to reality:
"What here is the essence that is permanent, stable, and eternal? This sense-field, being subject to change, is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
Having understood the sense-sphere of odors as the nose, and having reflected, "All this is not mine; I am not this," [one should dwell].
“This sphere of the nose and its odors is merely a product of conceptual construction, by which all foolish ordinary people of dull intellect are afflicted.
Thus he investigates this mode. (5.2.6.1) Furthermore, that monk searches for the sphere of the tongue:
“Dependent upon the tongue, dependent upon taste, and dependent upon the mental attention arising therefrom, ...”
Tongue-consciousness arises;
from the coming together of these three, contact occurs,
and [feeling] is co-nascent with contact.
Feeling, perception, and volition:
therein, feeling has the characteristic of experiencing;
perception has the characteristic of perceiving, taking signs as its object.

Thus, these phenomena, having arisen from their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), initiate distinct effects, yet all of them accomplish a single purpose.
For example: depending upon the channel (*nāḍī*), and...
Depending upon the tongs,
depending upon husked rice-water,
and depending upon the goldsmith, [gold is produced].
Or one finger-ring is made, or a hand ornament;
and all those phenomena are distinct from one another.
In the same way, in this case of the tongue-base,
he obtains both the tongue-sphere and the dharma-sphere of taste.
(5.2.6.2) Furthermore, that monk who perceives the reality of the tongue-base reflects in this manner:
“Is there anything in the sense base of the tongue and tastes that is permanent, pleasant, pure, or possessed of a self?
Examining in every way, he does not find even a single phenomenon, however subtle.
Endowed with such characteristics,
he becomes dispassionate toward the sense-sphere of the tongue and tastes:
"In that which this entire ocean of beings sinks and becomes impassioned..."
The five destinies—humans, gods, hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts—are mutually obstructed, submerged, and opposed to one another.
"He is liberated from the sense-base of the tongue and tastes: 'The sense-base of the tongue is not mine.'"
I am not the tongue-base;
I am not permanent, stable, eternal, or of an unchanging nature,
nor is the tongue-base.
“From that too, he becomes dispassionate.
(68) (5.2.7) Furthermore, that monk examines the sense-base of the body and its tangible objects. He sees: ‘Dependent upon the body, ...’”
Tangible objects arise, and from the coming together of these three, body-consciousness arises; from their conjunction, contact arises,
and simultaneously with contact, feeling, perception, and volition arise.
"These phenomena are to be understood as before.
Just as [the world] is [established] in the sense-faculties and bases regarding the eye-faculty, so too should it be understood regarding the body-tangible-base."
(5.2.8.1) Furthermore, that practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk, having surveyed the ten material spheres (*rūpy-āyatana*),
survey the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as one who sees the reality of the sphere of phenomena?
He sees, by means of knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye:

(5.2.8.2) “There are three phenomena included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*): analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*).”
In that regard, whatever is non-existent is subsumed under "phenomena" (dharma), and thus becomes the sphere of infinite space (ākāśāyatana).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is *nirvāṇa*.
"Deliberation" (*pratisaṅkhyā*) means that, having realized various kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*), one dwells [in it]. Having performed such deliberation, [one attains cessation].
It disperses, exhausts, and destroys the afflictions,
and it completely turns back all the outflows.
This is analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Non-discernment (*apratisaṅkhyā*) refers to that which is ignorance—that which does not know, does not penetrate, does not understand, does not fully awaken to, and does not reflect upon.
Hundreds of thousands of successive cognitions arise and perish:
the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses.
For those [factors] that have been destroyed, there is no further arising;
this is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The third is space (*ākāśa*).
These three dharmas are unborn and eternal. Even in terms of time, they have not been born, will not be born, and are not being born.
(5.2.9) Furthermore, how does that monk analyze the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) into two kinds?
What is form and what is non-form?

(5.2.10) “In that regard, the world of form consists of the ten material bases (*āyatana*). How, then, is visible and resistant form perceived by visual consciousness, which is invisible and non-resistant?”
In this way, how is sound apprehended by auditory consciousness, which is non-demonstrable and non-obstructive?
In this way, how is odor apprehended by olfactory consciousness, which is non-demonstrable and non-obstructive?
In this way, how is taste apprehended by gustatory consciousness, which is non-obstructive and non-demonstrable?
In this way, how is a tangible object apprehended by body-consciousness, which is itself non-demonstrable and non-obstructive?
Likewise, there are these five external bases and five internal bases.
How does the apprehension of these bases occur—those that are non-demonstrable and non-obstructive, as well as those that are demonstrable and obstructive?
(5.2.11.1) That monk sees:
"To the extent that there is a variety of objective supports, to that same extent a variety of consciousnesses arises."
It is like a seal and its impression.
In that regard, the seal is dissimilar [to its impression]:
the seal is hard, while the impression is soft; once heated, it becomes hard.
From both the hard and the non-hard, a counter-seal arises.
(70) In the same way, consciousness—which is invisible and non-obstructive—grasps an object that is visible and obstructive;
thus, a third counter-seal arises.
Of all dissimilar things, a dissimilar [result] is perceived;
thus, in the dissimilar, the dissimilar arises.
This is the first alternative.
(5.2.11.2) “The second alternative: like arises from like. For example: from white threads, a white cloth designated as a ‘garment’ is produced.”
(5.2.11.3) “The third alternative: that which arises from what is dissimilar. For example—fire from fire-sticks.”
A contradiction between wood and fire is observed.
(5.2.11.4) “The fourth alternative:
from the clear sky, a cloud is born.”

Just as thick curd arises from clear milk, so too do visual consciousness and the other types of consciousness arise from their respective specific causes and conditions, even though these factors—such as the visual consciousness itself—are dissimilar. ||
And there are verses on this point:
Delighting in the realization of the Dharma and dwelling in the pleasure grove of meditation,
one shall attain the supreme state through the awakening to the characteristics of reality.
For one who constantly delights in loving-kindness, is ever diligent in the sphere of the Dharma,
and knows the true nature of the characteristics of the body, is a monk in the ultimate sense.

(5.2.12.2) (71) He whose mind is directed toward the source [of existence] and is not destroyed by desire and anger—he should be known as a "monk" (*bhikṣu*); one who is the opposite of that is otherwise.
(5.2.12.3) Compassionate toward all beings and tranquil, free from all attachments and liberated from all bonds, he becomes a mendicant who knows reality.
(5.2.12.4) He whose discernment is workable and who is not struck down by sense objects—
stainless like gold and contented— he is called a monk.
He whose mind incurs no defilement through pleasant or unpleasant things should be known as one who follows the auspicious path, being entirely free from all faults.
One whose conduct is beyond reproach, who is devoted to righteousness, who has conquered the senses,
who is not deficient in limbs, and who possesses wisdom— such a person becomes a true mendicant.
(5.2.12.7) (72) He whose mind is always delighted in the teachings and in the understanding of the meaning of the teachings,
and who does not indulge in drinking or eating— that monk is one whose mind is at peace.
He whose mind finds delight in dwelling in forests and jungles, or on the ground strewn with grass in a cemetery— such a one is a true mendicant.
A monk who knows the true nature of the faults, who understands their results in particular,
and who knows the truth regarding causes and conditions, shall be free from all defilement.
One who has cleared the wilderness of evil, whose faults are destroyed, who has conquered the senses,
and who knows the method for ending rebirth— he is a monk with a tranquil mind.
One whose heart does not rejoice in praise and is not shaken by blame,
possessing a depth equal to the ocean— he is called a monk who knows yoga.
One who does not boast, is firm-minded, speaks gently, and is not greedy; who speaks at the proper time, is impartial, and is skillful—that monk is said to be peaceful.

(5.2.12.13) (73) One who knows reality, who understands the causes leading to the realm of desire as well as those leading to the realm of form and the formless realms, is called a monk learned in the scriptures.
One who is not attached to worldly talk, but is always intent on destroying faults,
for whom sense objects are like poison— he is taught by the Victors to be a true mendicant.
He whose mind is constantly like mud with regard to sensual desires—
he is wise, his mind is liberated, and he is freed from the bonds of saṃsāra.
(5.2.12.16) One who is devoted to the practice of meditation and study, from whom laziness is far removed,
and who acts for the benefit of sentient beings— such a one is called a forest-dwelling monk.

One who possesses the intelligence to answer questions, who acts with discernment, and has conquered the senses, should be known as a preacher of the Dharma; one who is the opposite of this is equal to grass.
(5.2.12.18) (74) He whose mind is not troubled in any way by physical fatigues,
who performs all necessary tasks and is intent on the welfare of the Saṅgha, should be known as such.

(5.2.12.19) He whose mind is set on the affairs of the Saṅgha— not for the sake of gain, nor for the sake of enjoyment, nor for the sake of fame, much less for any other reason— is liberated from all bonds.
He whose vow is not for the sake of all things, nor for gain, nor for fame,
but whose every action is for the sake of Nirvana— he is called a peaceful monk.
(5.2.12.21) Constantly abstaining from evil deeds and always delighting in virtuous actions,
a monk in the Buddha’s teaching should not associate with evil friends.
For one whose mind is cultivated with loving-kindness, who is skillful and upright in heart,
and who is unbroken in the precepts of training, nirvana is not far off.
(5.2.12.23) (75) For one who fears old age and death, who turns away from cyclic existence, and who meditates with heedfulness, nirvana is not far off.
(5.2.12.24) For one who knows the method for impermanence, who is skilled in the practices of emptiness and selflessness,
and who knows the method for the excellence of meditation, Nirvana is not far off. (5.2.12.25) (6.1) Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
How does that monk pass from the fifth stage-interval to the sixth stage-interval?
By means of knowledge consisting of what has been heard or by means of the divine eye, he sees:
that monk is resolved upon the fourfold alternatives.
“How is it that these phenomena are causes for similar things, dissimilar things for dissimilar things, and neither-similar-nor-dissimilar things for neither-similar-nor-dissimilar things?”
What are those that are half-similar?
(6.3.1) How are similar things causes for similar things?
For example: rice, being the cause, produces only rice.
In the same way, for pure internal karma, a corresponding fruit arises among gods and humans;
this is the first category.
(76) (6.3.2) “The causes of dissimilar things are themselves dissimilar.”
For example: from sweet milk, sour curd is produced.
In the same way, even internally, [suffering arises] from things that are dear and desired in this world, which are defiling, and from sounds, tangibles, tastes, forms, and smells.
Becoming sour like curd, an undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable ripening of the fruit arises among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals;
this is the second alternative.
(6.3.3) “There are no causes that are dissimilar, nor indeed are there any that are similar.”
For example: from the conjunction of blue and non-blue, a color called "unlike" arises.
In the very same way, regarding the internal ripening of the fruit of karma, it is neither similar to the fruit of karma, nor is the fruit similar to the karma.
For example: those who hold wrong views, such as the sacrificial priests, kill animals out of a desire for heaven;
by that [act], they go to hell; this is the third category.
(6.3.4) “Among things that are half-similar, half-similar causes come into being. From fine white threads, a coarse white cloth is produced;
and there exists a similar essence between the fine and the coarse.”
In the same way, causes that are partially similar produce results that are partially similar;
it is produced by subtle, unwholesome actions,
augmented by great hellish actions.
The fourth alternative:

(77) (6.4) Having reflected upon and observed the activity of coming and going according to the fruits of karma, that monk contemplates the fourfold division of the realms of existence as being like a wheel of karmic fruition:
“There may be karma that, though not yet reached, afflicts a person who belongs to a particular class of beings;
this is the first point.
There may be karma that, having been reached, afflicts persons.”
The second alternative:
there may be karma that afflicts both what has been reached and what has not been reached.
The third alternative: [there may be karma that afflicts neither].
There may be karma that afflicts neither when it has been reached nor when it has not been reached; this is the fourth alternative.
(6.5.1) “There exists such karma which, though not yet reached, afflicts one who belongs to a particular class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).”
Just as worldly people agree that the unpropitious constellation afflicts Kuru,
so too do those who transcend the world:
Karma that has not yet reached the ocean of visual consciousness afflicts a person with desire, grief, and so forth;
this is the first category.
(6.5.2) There may be karma which, having been reached, afflicts a person.
Just as fire, once reached, burns,
and a sword cuts— so it is with those who are mundane.
As for those who are supramundane:
Unwholesome karma that has been acquired afflicts beings in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
this is the second alternative.
(6.5.3) "There may be karma that, whether already acquired or not yet acquired, afflicts."
Just as knowledge restrains the power of poison, whether it has already taken effect or not yet taken effect; such is the case with worldly [remedies].
And those pertaining to the supramundane: the signs of shadows not yet reached in the hells at the time and place of death;
this is the third alternative.
(78) (6.5.4) “There may be a karma that neither when reached nor when not reached causes affliction;
for example, a medicinal seed that, though sown, is not yet reached [by the soil] and is thus incapable [of sprouting].”
Nor is it unattained; [this applies to] both worldly and supramundane [phenomena].

For example, even for an Arhat who remains as a monk, there are actions that must necessarily be experienced, such as actions equal in magnitude to Mount Sumeru, or actions that bring about the final nirvana of an Arhat; yet these do not cause affliction to the Arhat even when they are attained.
Actions belong to one who stands [in saṃsāra],
nor do they belong to one who is liberated;
this is the fourth alternative.
(6.6) "There may be karma to be experienced in the present life but not to be experienced in the next birth; this is the first alternative.
There may be karma to be experienced in the next birth but not to be experienced in the present life."
The second alternative:

there may be [karma] to be experienced upon rebirth and also to be experienced in the present life; the third alternative: [there may be karma to be experienced neither in the present life nor upon rebirth].
There may also be [karma] that is neither to be experienced in the present life nor to be experienced upon rebirth;
this is the fourth alternative.
(6.7.1) "What is that karma which is to be experienced in the present life but not to be experienced upon rebirth?"
Just as there is punishment for one who acts against the king,
[it is] "to be experienced in the present life, not to be experienced in a future birth"; this is the view of worldly people.
Regarding the transcendental benefits: by means of giving, one becomes praiseworthy among the virtuous;
being virtuous, one experiences happiness in this very life.
They do not go to the next world together with them; this is the first alternative.
(79) (6.7.2) "Could there be [karma] to be experienced upon rebirth that is also to be experienced in the present life?"
For example: "The attainment of heaven occurs by leaping into fire," so say the worldly people. The transcendent ones [say]:
"Whichever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is performed in this life, its result is experienced in another."
The perception of cause and fruit is seen;
this is the second alternative.
(6.7.3) “There may be [karma] to be experienced in the present life and also to be experienced upon rebirth.”

For example: that which is to be experienced in the present life becomes that which is to be experienced upon rebirth for worldly beings, as well as for those who are supramundane; this is the third alternative.
(6.7.4) “There may be that which is neither to be experienced in the present life nor to be experienced upon rebirth;
for example, ‘the vow of silence. Thus [it is said] by the worldly and the supramundane.
The action of one whose mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)— such as those who observe the vow of silence, practice generosity, or maintain moral discipline—
is neither experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) nor is its ripened fruit (*phalavipāka*) experienced in a future rebirth (*upapattivedanīya*).
The fourth alternative:

(6.8) "Thus, that monk, sitting in seclusion, having seen the vast web of the ripening of the fruits of karma with its many branches spread out among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans, dwells observing phenomena within phenomena as they truly are."
(80) (7.1) Furthermore, that practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within phenomena:
how does that monk become one who knows the ripening of the fruits of karma?
(7.2) Here, he becomes one who knows the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of the actions of beings.

For example: "These beings, being possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind; revilers of the noble ones and practitioners of wrong views—due to that cause and by that condition, upon the breakup of the body, they are reborn in states of woe, in the abysses, in the hells, or among animals or hungry ghosts."

(7.3) "Furthermore, these other beings were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; they did not revile the noble ones and practiced right view.
Because of that cause and because of that condition, upon the dissolution of the body, they have been reborn in a happy destination, among gods or humans.
(7.4) Contemplating and reflecting upon the ripening of the dharma of his own karma as it truly is, that monk—
Hearing from others,
he practices a conduct equal to that of sentient beings who have fallen under the domain of Māra;
he practices a conduct that culminates in nirvāṇa, which is world-wearying, auspicious, constantly diligent, directed toward the end of saṃsāra, and characterized by benevolence toward others.
For example: “May I deliver myself from cyclic existence, as well as the donors and masters of generosity.
(81) (7.5) That monk, knowing the ripening of karma and dharmas, reflects upon and calculates the ripening of karma and dharmas for hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans.
It is just as, for example, when a thread— whether blue, yellow, madder-red, or white— is seen within a clear and translucent beryl gem, appearing exactly as it truly is.
In the same way, that monk perceives with knowledge derived from hearing or with the purified divine eye the thread of ripening situated within the gem of karma.
Furthermore, that monk perceives through knowledge derived from hearing the ripening of the dharma of karma, which is like a gem:

"Just as there might be a certain gem that is white, pure, translucent throughout, without flaw, clear, capable of being pierced, workable, open on all sides, praised by all people, precious, and worthy of a king; and a king or a royal minister,
recognizing these qualities and knowing its value, [should take up] such a gem endowed with these virtues."
One should fasten it as an ornament for oneself.
(7.6.2) In this very way, that monk [should regard] these ten paths of wholesome action as a jewel in the bright fortnight.
It is pure on all sides, very clear, without blemish, irreproachable, and translucent;
it is capable of being pierced, being fit for piercing by the dharma-darts of objections, counter-objections, questions, and rejoinders regarding the side of the Dharma and its opposites;
and it is workable, in that one directs it toward generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom in whatever way one intends.
In whatever way he brings that jewel of the ten paths of wholesome action to a state of flexibility—

whether for the sake of the sovereignty of a universal monarch, or the sovereignty of a king of gods, or the sovereignty of Māra, or the sovereignty of Brahmā, or the sovereignty of the cultivation of outflow-free meditative absorptions and concentrations—
in that same way, this jewel of the true Dharma becomes flexible.
(7.6.3) "'With gates on all sides' means that there are gates on every side, serving as entrances for gods and humans.
Within those, this jewel of the True Dharma becomes a gate on all sides;
having emerged from the gates of saṃsāra,"
He enters the gate of *nirvāṇa*.

(7.6.4) "Praiseworthy by all people" means he is worthy of praise by those in training (*śaikṣa*) who possess right view. (7.6.5) "Worthy of a king" means he is fit for a lord of mind who understands how to practice the path of the true Dharma.
"Or for those who have entered [the path]—
thus he perceives this similarity between the *vaidūrya* gem endowed with all qualities and the gem of the True Dharma.
(7.7.1) Furthermore, that monk contemplates the ripening of karma and dharmas as being just like a gem:

“Just as another gem might be flawed— neither completely transparent, nor possessing all desirable qualities, nor white, nor capable of being pierced, nor workable, nor praised by all people, nor fit for a king or a royal minister—
(83) (7.7.2) even so is the dharma that resembles the Dharma of other sects, which is like a flawed gem.”
What is the wound?
It is the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
(7.7.3) "Not opening all doors" means it does not open the doors to hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
(7.7.4) “‘Not white’ means it is not endowed with the auspiciousness of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
(7.7.5) ‘Not capable of piercing’ means it is not capable of the probing-stick used by those who discourse on the Dharma through questions and counter-questions.

(7.7.6) ‘Not fit for a king or a royal minister’ means it is not fit for kings or lords of mind regarding the True Dharma—namely, for the eight types of persons (*pudgala*) who have entered and attained the True Dharma.”

(7.7.7) “Those who tie such a jewel of counterfeit dharma around their necks, having tied on that counterfeit jewel, wander through the beginningless cycle of existence among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Therefore, that monk [thinks]:
'Jewels are like jewels;
for example, having seen a golden jewel that resembles lapis lazuli,' "
The foolish common person thinks, "This is lapis lazuli.
(7.8) That monk, who knows the reality of the investigation into dharma and adharma, ascends to the seventh stage. Seeing that practitioner having ascended, [the gods think:]...
The terrestrial yakṣas, being delighted, announce it to the gods who roam the atmosphere;
they, in turn, to the four Great Kings; and they, to the gods belonging to the retinue of the four Great Kings.
They [belong] to the gods of the Thirty-three, they [belong] to Śakra,
and Śakra [belongs] to the Yāma gods.
The Yāmas [were the disciples] of the Tuṣitas;
the Tuṣitas were also [the disciples] of Maitreya;
and Maitreya was also [the disciple] of the gods who Delight in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).
The Nirmāṇaratis [also speak] to those who have power over the creations of others:
“Such-and-such a son of good family from Jambudvīpa... as before... (84) (7.9).
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
How does that monk perceive the ripening of the dharma of karma?
(7.10) “The eleventh form is that which is designated as non-informative (avijñapti). When one is engaged in the activity of all dharmas,”
And once he has taken up the restraint,
from that time forward, even while asleep, intoxicated, or heedless, a continuous flow of wholesome states proceeds for him,
just as the current of a river flows on constantly without ceasing.
Just as [the breath] flows for a person who is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted, so too does that form designated as "unmanifest" (avijñapti);
it is held to be invisible and non-obstructive.
But what, then, is that form? Its existence consists in karma;
therefore, that form also serves as a pillar for all wholesome dharmas.
That form is of eleven kinds.
(85) (7.11) That monk sees:
"How is it that these beings have various forms, various conditions, various destinies, and various types of physical bases?"
He sees: “Because these beings have diverse minds, diverse inclinations based on various supports, and perform diverse karmas,
therefore these beings have diverse forms, diverse conditions, diverse destinies, and diverse physical supports.”
Just as a skilled painter or a painter’s apprentice, having obtained a very white, firm, and delightful surface,
creates various beautiful forms with various colors and various designs according to his will—
so too is this mind. (86)

Just as a painter or a painter’s apprentice, acting with resolve, produces various mental paintings of sentient beings upon the ground of saṃsāra— which is exceedingly white, belongs to the three realms, is firm, consists in the ripening of the fruits of karma, and possesses various states, various destinies, and various types of physical bases— so too, he further creates a white form with white pigment.
With red [pigment] one makes it red; with yellow, one makes it yellow; with dove-grey, one makes it dove-grey.
Just as black [pigment] makes something black,

so too this painter of the mind, taking a white object as its basis, produces a white form among gods and humans— white dharmas that have not been drawn by the stains of outflowing passion and the like.
(7.12.3) “Taking up red dye as his pigment,
the painter of the mind produces a red form among gods and humans. ‘Red’ refers to desirable sounds, tastes, touches, forms, and smells on the canvas of the womb.”
(7.12.4) Furthermore, that painter of the mind, taking up yellow pigment,
produces beings belonging to the animal realm;
they too, through the power of their mutual yellow pigment, drink one another's blood.
“Overcome by passion, hatred, and delusion, they eat one another’s flesh and kill each other.
(7.12.5) Furthermore, that painter of the mind, seeing a pigeon as an object, [proceeds].
One performs soiled, pigeon-like karma that leads to the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

For their bodies resemble those scorched by a forest fire; they are overcome by hunger and thirst, overwhelmed by various sufferings, and—under the influence of the painter of the mind’s karma, with stinginess as their objective support—are shrouded in the darkness of delusion.
(87) (7.12.6) Furthermore, that painter of the mind, taking up black pigment as his material for action, paints black forms for the denizens of hell.

For they have been born there due to their black karma; they are bound within walls of glowing black iron, possessing black bodies, afflicted by various diseases, and subject to hunger and thirst—unlike anything else.
They are overcome by the suffering caused by their own past misdeeds. Furthermore, that monk, established in yoga: (7.12.7) [continues].

“That very same canvas of saṃsāra, consisting of the three realms, the five destinies, and the five colors, exists in three stages—the stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Therein, that painter of the mind, through the pursuit of sensual desires, paints various kinds of forms having the desire realm as their object.

With the brush of the four dhyānas, he then paints upon the form realm those twenty kinds of forms which rely on the objects of the form realm, are dissociated from desire, and are situated across sixteen levels.”
The mind, acting as a painter, depicts within the formless realm those things associated with the objects of the form realm— such as the four meditative attainments and so forth— as its focal points.
For this canvas of the three realms is indeed vast.
(7.13) Furthermore, that monk again sees the painter of the mind painting sentient beings in another manner:
"In this regard, the painter of the mind is like a painter;
the body is like a vessel of pigments."
Attachment, aversion, and delusion are like strong grass;
the object of focus is like a staircase;
and the sense faculties are like a brush.
External objects—sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—are like colors;
cyclic existence is like a wall;
and knowledge is like light.
The undertaking of vigor is like a hand.
Forms are like various paintings, produced from the growth of many types of dress, appearance, and clothing, and created by the ripening of the fruits of manifold karmas.
(7.14.1) Furthermore, that monk, absorbed in meditation, perceives that very painter of the mind in another manner:
"Just as that painter, if he remains untiring, has colors that are well-prepared, brushes that are bright and beautiful, and free from fear."
Then one paints beautiful forms;
in the very same way, if this painter of the mind is untiring, the various colors of meditative concentration (*dhyānaraṅga*) become well-prepared through the practice of meditation.
The objects of focus are like bright colors;
they are like beautiful brushes, comparable to the instructions mastered by a teacher who guides one on the path, being thoroughly mastered in their proper sequence.
Unwearied by drawing them in or pulling them away, that painter of the mind depicts beautiful forms upon the ground of meditative concentration.

(89) (7.14.2) “Then, becoming weary, that painter of the mind takes up the form of a hell-being, an animal, or a hungry ghost—whether belonging to the animal realm or otherwise—with an iron pestle and brush as the cause for the classes of rebirth in the unlovely states of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; having grasped these forms, he paints unlovely figures... [as detailed before] ... (7.15)
Furthermore, that monk observes the monkey-like mind as being like a monkey:
"Just as a monkey has an unrestrained movement, unhindered by various trees, creepers, flowers, fruits, forests, mountains, caves, chasms, and thickets;
even so, this monkey-like mind has an unrestrained movement throughout the five realms of existence."
The forests of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals are like various kinds of groves;
sentient beings are like trees;
and the creeper of craving is like many varieties of climbing vines.
Volitions are like flowers;
desirable and undesirable sounds, tastes, forms, and smells are like fruits;
the three elements are like those moving within the hollows of mountain caves.
The body is like a cave;
the monkey-like mind moves unimpeded through the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.
Like that monkey-like mind, it wanders through the grounds of saṃsāra.
(90) (7.16) Furthermore, that monk, absorbed in meditation, beholds the dancer of the mind as being like an actor:
“Just as an actor, having assumed various costumes, stage settings, garments, and musical instruments, performs a play;”
In this very way, this dancer of the mind assumes various costumes fashioned by diverse karmas across manifold planes— the planes of the classes of beings—
and wears various guises while bearing various kinds of causes and conditions;
its activities are like various kinds of musical instruments.

"His own realm as a drama" refers to the drama of saṃsāra. "Actor" refers to the actor that is the mind. "Drama" refers to [this] long, beginningless and endless saṃsāra, which consists of various and manifold types.

(7.17) Furthermore, that monk sees the fish of the mind like a fish in a river: “Just as a fish in a mountain torrent— turbulent with continuous waves, possessing a deep and swift current with a course of movement difficult to withstand, capable of sweeping away many trees, fierce in its activity with a continuous, rapid, and irresistible force— rises up and sinks down;”

In this very way, this fish of the mind [dwells] in the ocean of the three realms of existence, which is agitated by continuous waves, deep as the Vaitaraṇī river of the desire realm, and profoundly deep as the Avīci hell; it is a swift current, the current of virtuous and non-virtuous karma.

In the stream that is difficult to traverse—the stream of the five destinies which is difficult to cross for all the world’s foolish ordinary persons; in that which is "without movement," yet has movement throughout many eons; capable of dragging one along, with the swift current of sense objects.

"In the swift, continuous, irresistible, and fierce [river]" means: in the river of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which is fierce with its continuous and irresistible force of impermanence (*anityatā*), the fish of the mind performs its surfacing and submerging;
it surfaces among gods and humans, and...
“The fish of the mind sinks in the river of craving among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
(7.18) Furthermore, that practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does a monk established in yoga, knowing the ripening of the phenomena of karma, perceive all sentient beings as being dependent upon the mind?
Does he see beings who are subject to the mind, obedient to the mind, and deceived by the mind?
He sees them through knowledge consisting of what has been heard or with the divine eye:
"All sentient beings are dependent upon the activity of the mind."
The destinies of the mind’s activity are dependent upon the mind.
And how are these sentient beings liberated from this beginningless and endless saṃsāra, which involves wandering through many realms of existence?
He perceives this through knowledge derived from hearing or with the divine eye:
“By the defilement of the mind, all sentient beings are bound; by the purification of the mind, they are liberated.
(92) (7.20) In this context, the mind is of many kinds, distinguished by its variety of objects and its variety of intrinsic natures.

It is fivefold according to the division of realms and destinies within the five destinies. It carries the yokes; it is conjoined with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*), as well as with the formations (*saṃskāra*) associated with the mind;
and it is not conjoined with the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena—space and so forth—which are eternal. Thus, it is of five kinds according to the distinction of its supreme bases.
That [craving] is immeasurable due to the distinction of the sense faculties.
Due to the distinction of the various bases of craving, there are five types of consciousness.
In brief, this is the side belonging to the defiled category.
(7.21.1) How does the side of purification come about?
There are three antidotes for the three root afflictions,
which have been taught as the true path by the words of all the past and future perfectly awakened Buddhas.
Namely: for passion, the meditation on the foul; for hatred, loving-kindness;
for delusion, dependent origination.
In that regard, attachment arises toward the body;
taking that very body as his object, he dwells upon it and analyzes it.
Starting from the toenails up to the head, he analyzes the gross parts and sub-parts [of the body], thinking: "Who am I, or what is mine within these regions of my own limbs?
He perceives the toenail as a separate body.
“The nail is not the body; the toes of the feet are not the body, nor am I.”
Wherever this "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra) exists, there is no body; nor does this "I-maker" exist in the soles of the feet,
nor in the ankles or the calves, nor is it the body.
I am not the heel, nor the body;
I am not the mass of the heel, nor the circle, nor the body.
I am not the hip-bone, nor the body; I am not the anus, nor the body; I am not the forty-five bones located in the back, nor the body.
The bones of the neck and limbs are not the body, nor am I.
The bones within the mouth are not the body, nor am I.
The bones within the skull are not the body.
Or again, having analyzed it thoroughly, a monk does not perceive the body as being a separate entity.
Nor does one perceive the body by means of each [sense] individually, nor does one perceive the body as something separate.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not the body of the self.
Nor does he perceive the self within them;
rather, he analyzes the body into its individual atoms and sees his own body as being like mustard-seed-sized powder.
He analyzes the great elements: "Who am I?
Am I the earth element, am I the water element?"
"I am the fire element; I am the air element"?
He does not perceive the self as an element.
Nor, while perceiving the element within the self,
does one perceive it as being a separate entity from the ultimate standpoint;
just as, for example, one perceives a forest as a collection of many trees.
A forest does not exist by means of a single tree; nor does a so-called "forest" exist in ultimate reality;
there is no forest apart from the trees.
Even a tree, when divested of its bark, roots, branches, leaves, and shoots, does not exist as a distinct entity;
it does not exist in ultimate reality (paramārtha).
However, by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya), the forest exists.
In the same way, this body is merely a collection of hands and so forth;
it is called "body" only conventionally.
One who knows the true nature of the body's phenomena becomes detached from the body.
One becomes dispassionate even toward the limbs of the body,
and one becomes dispassionate even toward all the elements of sensation and the sense faculties.
For a mind that is dispassionate, the craving that leads to renewed existence, which is accompanied by delight and lust, no longer afflicts it.
In this way, he exerts himself as an antidote to attachment.
How does he exert himself as an antidote to aversion?
He becomes established in loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
“Alas, these beings are in distress, namely: that they are born, die, pass away, and are reborn within the five destinies;
(95) they are beset by the five fears! Toward those who are like the dead, compassion arises as toward a mother.
“How could one direct anger—which is like pouring caustic acid upon a wound—toward beings who are thus suffering, when those beings are already afflicted by their very nature?
Thus he dwells, repeatedly striking down that second great affliction.
(7.21.4) Furthermore, how does that monk exert himself toward the antidote for the third great affliction?
“Enshrouded by delusion, sentient beings engage in misconduct of body, engage in misconduct of speech, and engage in misconduct of mind.”
Upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in states of deprivation, in the lower realms, in the hells.
But when they are free from delusion and preceded by right view,
they then practice good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
They become knowers of the reality of dharma and adharma.
And when they possess the discernment that knows the reality of dharma and adharma,
then there is an absence of the third, which is great affliction.
(7.22) That monk [thought]: "In this way, there are three antidotes for the three afflictions.
Through their destruction, all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) [are eliminated]. (96)
The destruction of the bases occurs;

just as from the destruction of a tree’s root, its bark, roots, leaves, foliage, trunk, branches, flowers, fruits, and so forth, all completely wither or perish, even so, through the slaying of those three, there is the slaying of all afflictions.
(8.1) Furthermore, that practitioner of yoga dwells observing phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk pass from the seventh stage-interval to the eighth stage-interval?
He perceives this through knowledge consisting of what has been heard or with the divine eye:
How does that monk see the eye as it truly is from the very beginning?
(8.2) "How is it that among all forms to be cognized, the foolish commoner becomes attached, becomes dispassionate, or becomes deluded?
In that regard, seeing a friend, he becomes attached."
Having seen a form that is a basis for passion, such as a woman or something else,
he gives rise to passion; or toward things that are bases for hatred, such as an enemy or something resembling an enemy, he gives rise to hatred.
Those whose eyes are shrouded by passion and hatred do not see form as it truly is.
One whose mind is shrouded by delusion—the foolish worldling—becomes attached, repelled, or bewildered regarding those objects cognizable by the eye, which are mere conceptual constructs.
Deceived by craving, such persons delight themselves by means of their own self through their own arbitrary imaginings.

(97) (8.3) “For example, it is like a dog that seizes a bone stripped of its flesh and thrusts it into its mouth; with its teeth, it gnaws at the bone, which has entered the cavity of its mouth and is soaked by the flowing saliva.

From the mouth of that excessively greedy dog, blood flows from the gaps between his teeth; he thinks, "This is not [the blood] of another," and does not think: "This is my own blood, which I myself am tasting."
Greedy for flavor, that dog even devours its own tongue;
enveloped by greed for flavor, it perceives the unstable as substantial,
though it is merely a product of conceptual construction.
(8.4) “In the very same way, the foolish common person becomes attached to forms cognizable by the eye— those forms that are pleasing to the eye.

With his mind shrouded by the saliva of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and established upon investigation (*vicāra*), he casts them into the mouth resembling the eye and devours them in such a manner that the blood of craving flows from him.”
Greedy for the blood-like essence of craving, one considers "this is mine" to be beautiful;
thus, one finds gratification therein.
In this regard, foolish ordinary people are like dogs.
As are the bones, so are the forms cognizable by the eye; as are the discursive thoughts, so is the gnawing upon skin and bone; as are the teeth, so are the sense objects.
Therefore, forms cognizable by the eye are like skeletons, serving as deceivers for all foolish ordinary persons.
(98) (8.5) Furthermore, that monk reflects: "How do monks, terrified by the fear of craving and weary of cyclic existence, abandon all sensual desires?"
It is just as when an elephant sixty years of age is bound by fivefold bonds, attended by men who are skilled trainers of elephants, that great-bodied one confined within a cage;
he receives an abundance of sugarcane, lumps of sugar, sweetmeats, and the taste of rum for drinking.
And his diversion is provided with the sounds of musical instruments and songs, so that he might forget the pleasures of the forest;
having forgotten them, he would dwell here among ordinary elephants and become subject to the control of others.
Then that noble elephant, even while being thus attended to, did not cease from wandering in his own beloved forest happiness;
reflecting upon the mountain groves, the flowers and fruits of the woods, the songs of the birds, the delightful river cascades, and the various regions of the earth,
he remained mindful of those joys despite being bound by all his fetters.
Having severed all bonds,
disregarding men as mere noble elephants,
and having shattered the cage of the household;
Having drunk the flavorful beverage of abundant sugarcane, jaggery, sweetmeats,
and rum, he cannot be deceived by songs and instrumental music,
nor can any diversion be created for his mind.
He does not find pleasure in the comforts of the forest,
nor does he wish to attain equality with ordinary elephants;
he returns once more to the forest.
(8.6) "In this way, a monk who practices yoga is bound by five fetters that have operated since beginningless time.
By which five?
Namely, by pleasant sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells."
By which persons—like well-bred elephants—is he mounted?
Namely, by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousnesses associated with affliction;
thus he is confined within the cage of the house of his own intellect.
Namely: being confined within a house by children, wife, gardens, female and male slaves, and enjoyments;
the phrase "the taste of drinking abundant sugarcane, sweetmeats, and *sīdhu* liquor" is a designation for the drinking of passion (*rāga*) that produces the joy of conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*).

One whose intellect is attached to craving and who has shattered the passion for delight—being like one who is "equal to song and instrumental music"—should be "equal to ordinary elephants. This is a designation for elephants that are false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

"He should dwell together with them" means that he takes pleasure in the sweet-sounding discourses of false views, which are associated with the ordinary persons (*prākṛtapuruṣa*) who are possessed of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
"Led by others" is a designation for one who is dependent on passion, hatred, and delusion.
"A well-bred elephant" is a designation for a practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*).
"Even while being served" is a designation for that which pertains to all defilements and has fallen into delusion.
Having recollected the mountain of deliverance (*nairyāṇika-parvata*), [one understands that] "mountain groves" (*parvata-kuñjā*) is a designation for the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*).
Flowers, fruits, and so forth are the productions of the mind of the true path.
"Nirvāṇa" refers to that which has become the fruit.
"The cries of birds" is a metaphor for the cries of those who preach the Dharma.
"Delightful with streams and waterfalls" is a designation for the river of wisdom.
‘Nirjhara’ (the mountain stream) is a designation for the one-pointed mind.
‘Bhūmibhāga’ (the ground) is a designation for the dwellings of the Brahmās, namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
"Having reflected," that is, having reflected upon the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
that practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) runs toward the monastery. (8.7) "Therefore, one should become a practitioner of yoga who is like an elephant."
Not by way of a simile for tomorrow.
(100) (9.1) Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk ascend from the eighth stage-interval to the ninth stage-interval?
With knowledge consisting of hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
(9.2) "All this triple world is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, like a vessel of impurity"; he also sees all sensual desires as such.
“It is as if, in the midst of a forest thicket, there were a date-palm tree in a great mountain chasm,
requiring hundreds of unequal hardships to reach;
and at its very top, there would be only a few fruits.”
They are difficult to reach and fraught with many dangers:

through the danger of falling into abysses, they cause uncertainty regarding life; and through the danger of hollows, those situated even on the upper branches of a tree are liable to fall and lose their lives.
Then a man might go forth—
a deluded, foolish worldling, blinded by greed for flavors—
and he would see those fruits.
He does not take pleasure in the destruction of life by falling into a chasm or from the top of a tree into a hollow;
yet that foolish, ordinary person of dull intellect, being carried away by the taste of a meager flavor, climbs that very tree.
From that tree—
Without having reached those fruits, he would fall;
he would lose his life.
Or, if by some other means or by ordinary action he does not fall, [he will reach them].
Bound entirely by the passion for flavors, one of childish intellect does not perceive the manifold dangers.
(101) (9.3) In the very same way, that monk sees: "The five openings of the realms of existence are like the hollows within a forest; they are great abysses equal to all the afflictions."
"Date tree" is a designation for the tree of desire.
"Hundreds of unequal [thorns]" is a designation for the hundreds of thousands of individual afflictions and the sufferings of seeking them.
"'Fruits hanging at the edge of the tree'" is a designation for the desired sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells of those whose minds are attached to all sensual pleasures.
"Difficult to obtain" means that the fruits of sensual desire are difficult to attain;
for instance, they are acquired through entering the ocean, through the turmoil of warfare, or through the hardships of serving kings, thievery, trade, and so forth.
"Abounding in faults," which refers to the fruits of sensual desire, is a designation for passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
"Falling into a chasm" is a designation for the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts.
"There is a danger to one's life" is a designation for the life of the Dharma. "The defect of a hollow" is a designation for that which is empty, void, insubstantial, and pithless.
“A man might come” (102)— this is a designation for the fool who holds wrong views.
Therefore, having seen that sensual pleasures are like fruit abounding in many defects and possess little relish, [one should renounce them].
That monk does not form conceptual attachments to any sensual desires.
Furthermore, that monk views sensual desires as being like the crest of a flame:
"Just as a lamp is pleasing to the sight but possesses an extremely sharp touch."
A foolish moth might see a beautiful lamp;
it would fall into that lamp and meet its destruction.
In this very way, foolish ordinary beings— moths shrouded by passion, hatred, and delusion— behold all the delightful objects of desire as if they were lamps.
Thus, if they fall into that lamp of desire, like moths, they are burned in the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Therefore, 'Enough with sensual desires!'—thus that monk becomes dispassionate toward sensual desires. Furthermore, that monk dwells contemplating phenomena among internal phenomena:
'By what fetters are sentient beings bound that they run on and wander through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)?"
(9.6.1) He sees, by means of knowledge derived from hearing or with the divine eye:
"This world is bound by two bonds: by the bond of nutriment and by the bond of contact."

(9.6.2) “In that regard, by means of the fourfold bond of nutriment: namely, edible food consisting of morsels, mental volition as nutriment, nutriment consisting of meditative absorption, and nutriment consisting of contact. (9.6.3) What are edible foods consisting of morsels?”
Namely: the four abodes of men, the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm, and the eight great hells.

Furthermore, some hungry ghosts and animals [subsist on] the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*). (9.6.4) “Fish and those of similar kind [subsist on] the nutriment of mental volition.
(9.6.5) The gods of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) subsist on the nutriment of meditative absorption (*dhyānāhāra*).”
(103) (9.6.6) “Birds are sustained by the nutriment of touch; so too are snakes and others of that kind, who are deceived by sexual union through touch.”
(9.6.7) “All foolish ordinary persons in the desire realm—whether humans, pretas, animals, or those in hell—who constitute this desire realm through the indulgence of sensual desires;
(9.6.8) “whereas the formless realms are sustained by the attainment, the object of focus, and nutriment.
(9.6.9) “Thus, in this way, this world is bound by two things.”
Thus, through dispassion, one is not liberated from all the bonds of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
(9.7.1) He perceives the eye as it truly is in another manner, as well as the forms cognizable by the eye.
Furthermore, there is that karma which arises from eye-contact, which is conducive to pleasure, has pleasure as its objective support, yet results in the ripening of non-pleasure.
He understands that also as it truly is.

Likewise, he understands as it truly is that visual object cognizable by the eye which is a basis for mental distress, and even that action born of eye-contact which, having suffering as its objective support, results in a pleasant ripening.
He understands that also as it truly is.

Which is that form cognizable by the eye that has happiness as its object but results in the ripening of unhappiness? It is one who, in this very Dharma, contemplates phenomena among internal phenomena.

With the eye, one who engages in improper mental attention perceives a visible form as an object; he contemplates it, relishes it, and recognizes it as "pleasure. Yet, through its transformation, it results in the ripening of suffering, leading to rebirth among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Which is that action which has a ripening of suffering in the present but a ripening of happiness through transformation?
Here, having seen forms cognizable by the eye,
one whose mind is directed toward appropriate mental attention born of eye-contact does not become attached to them.
He does not direct his mind [toward it].
Consequently, this results in the ripening of suffering in the present, yet it is conducive to future happiness, leading to rebirth among gods or humans, and culminating in nirvana.
(9.7.2–6) Likewise regarding phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
(10.1) Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga dwells contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena:
how does that monk dwell with equanimity toward forms cognizable by the eye?

In this case, a monk, having seen forms with the eye, is neither attracted nor repelled; he does not gaze longingly, nor does he revile; he does not crave them and does not direct his mind toward them.
He is not obscured by improper mental attention.
He becomes equanimous;
he perceives a state conducive to equanimity, not a state conducive to suffering or pleasure.

(105) (10.2) Furthermore, that monk ascends to the tenth stage-interval, which consists of the transformation of six stages— namely, the interval between the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna, as well as the four dhyānas.
He ascends to this transformation of the six stages.
He perceives the arising and passing away of phenomena;
he knows the arising and passing away of phenomena.
By means of the Noble Eightfold Path, the way leading to cessation, he exerts himself to enter and attain the gate of Nirvana.
(106) (10.3) As he was thus striving, the terrestrial yakṣas, seeing that the bonds of Māra were for the most part deceptive, rejoiced and announced it to the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere.
They, in turn, announced it to the four Great Kings.
They, in turn, inform the gods of the Four Great Kings;
the gods of the Four Great Kings inform the gods of the Thirty-three;
and the gods of the Thirty-three inform the Yāma gods.
The Yāma gods [aspire] to the Tuṣita heaven;
the Tuṣita gods to the Nirmāṇarati heaven; and the Nirmāṇarati gods to the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven.
They announce this to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods and the Brahmakāyika gods as follows:
"A son of good family from Jambudvīpa... [as before in detail] ... has ascended to the eighth stage-interval and has entered within the six stages."
And having ascended it, he said:
(10.4) "Then, having heard this, the gods of the Brahma-realm were supremely delighted; abandoning their dwelling in the bliss of meditative concentration, they [approached]."
Then, having heard what has occurred, they become even more joyful.
And there are verses on this subject:
The certainty of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions is that everything one has done oneself is experienced; for embodied beings are indeed bound by their own karma.
The stages of affliction are sweet at first but bitter in their maturation;
they should indeed be avoided like poison, for they bring about every kind of misfortune.
One should not fall under the power of the afflictions nor within the range of ignorance;
for one who possesses wisdom enjoys happiness both in this world and in the next.
The afflictions are always to be destroyed by wisdom, just as grass is destroyed by fire;
therefore, wisdom is the supreme Brahman, which reveals the Three Jewels.
(10.5.4) Those who delight in the sphere of knowledge abide on the path of peace;
but those who have been bitten by the serpents of the afflictions—all of them have gone to destruction.
Those wise and virtuous ones who know the higher and the lower, who perceive reality as it is, go to the supreme state, which is free from old age and death.
But those who delight in cyclic existence and take pleasure with the enemies that are the afflictions,
being bound by eternal fetters, they wander in the perilous straits of becoming.
(10.5.7) For one whose intellect is directed toward liberation and whose conduct is always auspicious,
that assembly of gods is ordained for him, as is the world of Brahmā.
He for whom passion and the like are objects of aversion, and the Buddhas and the like are always objects of veneration—
he destroys cyclic existence just as fire consumes dry fuel.
(10.5.9) (108) He who is not under the sway of the mind, but whose mind always follows him— he destroys the afflictions, just as the rising sun dispels the darkness.
The mind is the supreme enemy; no other enemy is so reckoned.
Beings are always consumed by the mind, just as trees are consumed by fire at the end of time.
(10.5.11) For that fool, deluded and with senses unsubdued, who has fallen under the power of the mind, there is no cessation of suffering; for him, Nirvana is far away.
For one who understands suffering, the ripening of suffering, and the cause of suffering,
all bonds and the entire multitude of afflictions perish from every side.
The supreme knowledge of lights is said to be delusion for those in darkness;
therefore, he who delights in light is called a wise man.
The wise person should abandon delusion, for it brings about all misfortune;
for one who has fallen under the power of delusion, there is no peace.
(10.5.15) One would rather touch a blazing fire or dwell with serpents than be joined with afflictions, if one desires one's own welfare.
(10.5.16) (109) Knowledge is the supreme among immortals, the highest treasury of all that is auspicious;
it is the ultimate kinsman among kinsmen and the most excellent wealth among all riches.
Therefore, one should constantly burn away the mountains of afflictions with the fire of knowledge;
for one whose mountains of afflictions have been consumed, the state of bliss is firmly established.
Blinded men of dull intellect sink into darkness—
those who do not feel revulsion for saṃsāra, that cage of unrighteousness.

(10.5.19) For those whose intellect is undeceived, their birth is indeed fruitful; and they, whose minds are always fixed on the Dharma, are always worthy of honor by the virtuous. (10.5.20) (110) (10.6) Thus that monk, knowing the rules of Dharma and non-Dharma, dwells having become truly virtuous.
For him whose mind is thus perfectly pure:
"The many hundreds of thousands of peaks of the mountain of saṃsāra crumble, are vomited forth, and perish; they shall not come into being again."
“His enemies, the afflictions, perish, and nirvāṇa draws near to him. (111)
